Consequently the marginal-tail parameter of Lemma <a href="#lem:tail" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:tail">5</a> is at most $CnD(\log n)^C$. At the target itself it is at most $Cn(\log n)^C$. The latter bound shows that the width $w=n^{3/5}$ has failure mass at most $n^{-100}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. In fact its tail is bounded by $C\exp[-c n^{1/10}/(\log n)^C]$.

<a id="scanner:Q-definition"></a>
At a charge round write $h$ for an old joint history, of probability $w_h$, and $\sigma_{h,u}$ for its transported state in Proposition <a href="#prop:transport" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:transport">23</a>. Let $\mu_\sigma$ denote the coherent probability measure of Lemma <a href="#lem:symbol" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:symbol">19</a>. The entropy derivative uses the old-history weights $w_h$; the same transported states occur in the energy estimate with terminal weights $(1-p)w_h$. We therefore measure the entropy cost of the old splits by $\mathcal Q(p)$, defined as $$\sum_{h\ {\mathrm{good}}}w_h
  \int_{\mathbb R}m_s(u)
   \int\sum_{i\ {\mathrm{split\ in}}\ h}
       \eta_{i,h}(\theta)\,d\mu_{\sigma_{h,u}}(\theta)\,du.
 \label{scanner:Q-definition}$$ Each split term in this sum has a unique splitting band, and its partition $P,Y,F$ is understood to be that band’s partition. If term $i$ splits on the near side, its moved set is $x=Y\cap\widetilde X_i$, the unassigned part of its designated $r_0$-ball, and $\eta_{i,h}=S_\theta(x\mid P)+S_\theta(x\mid Y\setminus x)$; on the far side exchange $P,F$. These quantities are nonnegative. They are also bounded by $C(\log n)^C$, because the moved sites lie in an $r_0$-ball. The measure $m_s(u)\,du$ has fixed finite mass $2s$.

<a id="scanner:charge-gain"></a>
On every good old history each split term is sampled with probability at least $c/(nD)$, and its sampled move has exactly the corresponding $\eta_{i,h}$. Equation <a href="#transport:entropy-gain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="transport:entropy-gain">[transport:entropy-gain]</a> therefore gives, at a charge round, $$-\partial_p\log N^2
 \ge \frac{cka}{nD}\mathcal Q(p)
       -CkaK a^{1/4}(\log n)^C-O_{\rm fixed}(\log(k+2)).
 \label{scanner:charge-gain}$$ At fill rounds retain just the same negative error; the entropy gains are nonnegative. Here and below “fixed” means that the complete single-copy instance and the scanner have been fixed. No such constant survives the replica limit.

<a id="scanner:selected-density"></a>
Integrate over every full round, including fills. Adjacent endpoint metrics agree by construction, so the left sides telescope. Initially $-\log N^2\ge-O_{\rm fixed}(\log(k+2))$: the floor <a href="#replicas:leaf-floor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="replicas:leaf-floor">[replicas:leaf-floor]</a> passes to the initial mean tree by Lemma <a href="#transport:means" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="transport:means">20</a>, and $\|\mathrm{pre}\|\le1$. At the last endpoint the rough upper comparison <a href="#comparator:rough-upper" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="comparator:rough-upper">[comparator:rough-upper]</a> gives $$-k^{-1}\log N^2
 \le 2\log d_*-\log z+C_eW(nL^e+nD+n)+o_k(1)
 \le C_eW n^{1+e}+o_k(1).$$ For the last inequality use $\kappa\le e$, $L\le n$, and $\log d_*=S_{\widetilde\Omega}(X)+O(w+|\log z|)$. Restrict the positive charge integrals in <a href="#scanner:charge-gain" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:charge-gain">[scanner:charge-gain]</a> to $[\epsilon/2,\epsilon]$, but pay the negative errors on all $2nm$ full rounds. Since $aK=W$, the integrated inequality, normalized by the number of charge rounds, is $$\frac1{nm}\sum_{\text{charge rounds}}
  \int_{\epsilon/2}^{\epsilon}\frac{\mathcal Q(p)}{KnD}\,dp
 \le C_e\left(\frac{n^e}{m}+a^{1/4}(\log n)^C\right)+o_k(1).$$ The interval has length $\epsilon/2$, and $m\asymp n^\mu$. Averaging therefore gives a charge round and a $p_k$ in this interval such that $$\frac{\mathcal Q(p_k)}{KnD}\le\delta_n+o_k(1).
 \label{scanner:selected-density}$$ The fixed factor two in the interval length is absorbed into constants. All integrands are bounded at fixed $k$, and continuous in the interior interpolation parameter, so ordinary averaging suffices for this selection.

Apply the energy estimate <a href="#transport:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="transport:energy">[transport:energy]</a> at this same point. For each term its split weight is at most $CD/m$. There are at most $CKnD$ split term occurrences in each joint leaf. On old good leaves the transported states are exactly those in <a href="#scanner:Q-definition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:Q-definition">[scanner:Q-definition]</a>; their full terminal weight differs only by the factor $1-p_k\le1$. Hölder’s inequality, applied to the positive measure over histories, terms, $u$, and $\theta$, bounds their sum of $\eta^{1/8}$ by $$CKnD\bigl(\delta_n+o_k(1)\bigr)^{1/8}.$$ On bad old histories use the uniform local dimension bound and Lemma <a href="#scanner:histories" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:histories">25</a> with an arbitrarily large fixed tail power. On all new leaves use the same dimension bound and their total terminal weight $p_k\le\epsilon$. After increasing the fixed logarithmic power, the energy estimate is therefore $$\langle v_k,\overline{\widetilde H}v_k\rangle
 \le 2\widetilde E_0+
 C a^2\frac Dm KnD(\log n)^C
       \bigl(\delta_n^{1/8}+\epsilon+n^{-100}\bigr)+o_k(1).$$ The factors in this expression have distinct origins: $D/m$ is the split probability of one fixed term, $KnD$ counts split occurrences, and $a^2$ is the local skew cost. Their product simplifies to $$a^2\frac Dm KnD
   =\frac{W^2nD^2}{mK}
   \le CW^2n^\ell D^2.$$ Subtracting $\widetilde E_0$ and dividing by $\widetilde g\ge g/2$ proves <a href="#scanner:energy-output" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:energy-output">[scanner:energy-output]</a>.

Only splitting terms contribute to this energy error; all others have zero skew exactly. Thus its coefficient contains no total-volume factor. The symbol remainders can be summed over all terms before taking $k\to\infty$, because that complete term set is finite and fixed. Their uniformity in replica states and in the interpolation parameter also justifies the possibly $k$-dependent selection in <a href="#scanner:selected-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:selected-density">[scanner:selected-density]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-53"></a>
#### Geometric targets and entropy inputs

We now supply the scanner’s geometric and entropy inputs for unions of rectangles and triangles. These include the geometric targets of the final tiling, whose number of pieces may grow with the scale. The constant $D_0$ and the function $F_{\rm box}$ are those of Proposition <a href="#prop:initial-box" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:initial-box">7</a>. Fix the numerical constant $C_{\rm tpl}$ large enough to absorb the layer-count constant in the proof below. The entropy bounds will be reused each time the safe-box exponent improves.

<a id="stmt-scanner-template"></a>
<div id="scanner:template" class="definition">

**Definition 27** (A template). Let $s_0\ge1$ and $n$ be positive integers. A template with parameters $(n,s_0)$ is a nonempty finite set $T\subset\mathbb Z^2$ of the form $$T=\bigcup_{a=1}^{N_0}(P_a\cap\mathbb Z^2),
 \qquad n\ge C_{\rm tpl}N_0(s_0+1),
 \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{diam}}_\infty T\le n,$$ where $N_0\ge1$ is an integer and each $P_a$ is a closed convex rectangle or triangle of sup-norm diameter at most $s_0$, all of whose sides have slope $0,\infty,1$, or $-1$. Empty sampled pieces can be omitted. For the fixed cut $A$, the template is separated from the cut if $$\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(T,Z)>4D_0s_0.$$ As above, $T_j$ is the ambient integer dilation, $X=A\cap T$, and $Q_j=A\cap(T_j\setminus T)$, for $j\ge0$.

</div>

The diameter condition merely fixes a convenient common size parameter. The estimates below use the number and sizes of the pieces, rather than convexity of their union. They therefore allow the disconnected fragments which occur in the later tiling.

<a id="stmt-scanner-templates"></a>
<div id="scanner:templates" class="lemma">

<a id="scanner:template-geometry"></a>
<a id="scanner:template-entropy"></a>
**Lemma 28** (Rows, coverings, and shell entropy). *For $C_{\rm tpl}$ sufficiently large, a template satisfies $$|T|\le Cns_0,\qquad
 |T_j\setminus T_{j-1}|\le n\quad(1\le j\le s_0),
 \qquad |\partial_{\mathbb Z^2}T_j|\le Cn\quad(0\le j\le s_0).
 \label{scanner:template-geometry}$$ Suppose it is separated from the cut and, for some $0<e<1$, $F_{\rm box}(r)\le C_e r^{1+e}$ for every integer $r\ge1$. Then, for every integer $1\le L\le s_0$, $$S_\Omega(X)\le C'_e ns_0^e,\qquad
 S_\Omega(Q_j)\le C'_e nL^e\quad(0\le j\le L).
 \label{scanner:template-entropy}$$ The same shell bound, with an additional $Cn$, holds for any prefix obtained by including all depth rows before one row and an arbitrary subset of that last row. All physical cuts of $X,Q_j$, and $A\cap T_j$ have $O(n)$ edges.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-scanner-templates"><summary>Proof of stmt-scanner-templates</summary>

*Proof.* Consider first one sampled piece. On an integer horizontal row its sites form an integer interval. Its left endpoint is a maximum of affine integer-valued functions with slopes in $\{-1,0,1\}$, and its right endpoint is a minimum of such functions; horizontal sides impose an interval constraint on the row index. To obtain these formulas, round the intercepts of the defining line inequalities. Because the slopes are integers, this rounding is independent of the integer row index. The difference of the lower and upper bounds is convex, so the nonempty rows are consecutive. On consecutive nonempty rows each endpoint moves by at most one. Consecutive row intervals overlap or are adjacent as integer intervals.

After integer sup-norm dilation by $j$, the interval on a row is the union of the original intervals in the window of rows at distance at most $j$, each extended by $j$ on both ends. This union is still an integer interval. Its endpoints are the sliding minimum and maximum of the old endpoints, minus or plus $j$. They again move by at most one between consecutive nonempty rows: the nonempty index windows at two consecutive rows have Hausdorff distance at most one, and the old endpoint functions are 1-Lipschitz. One more dilation changes each endpoint on an old row by at most two and adds at most two rows, each of length $O(s_0+j+1)$. This proves a bound $C(s_0+j+1)$ for both the new layer and the edge boundary of one piece. Summing over the pieces proves <a href="#scanner:template-geometry" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:template-geometry">[scanner:template-geometry]</a>, with the layer constant absorbed in $C_{\rm tpl}$. The area bound follows from $|P_a\cap\mathbb Z^2|\le C(s_0+1)^2$.

<a id="scanner:mixed-piece"></a>
We also need a count at intermediate dyadic scales. In the usual dyadic partition of the lattice into integer squares, the number of side-$u$ squares containing both a site of a dilated piece and a site outside it is $$O\bigl((s_0+j+1)/u+1\bigr),\qquad u\ge1.
 \label{scanner:mixed-piece}$$ Indeed, in a block of $u$ consecutive nonempty rows the two endpoints vary by at most $u$. Only constantly many square columns near each endpoint can be mixed. At the first and last blocks count instead the whole width, which costs $O((s_0+j+1)/u+1)$ in total. A square mixed for a union, or for a difference of two unions, must be mixed for at least one of the constituent sets. Thus the corresponding count for $T$, $T_j$, or $T_j\setminus T$, with $j\le s_0$, is at most $C(N_0+n/u)$.

Cover $T_j\setminus T$ by maximal contained dyadic squares, with side capped at the largest power of two not exceeding $L$. These squares partition the set: a single site is an admissible square, and the dyadic nesting makes distinct maximal squares disjoint. At the cap there are at most $Cn/L$ squares because $|T_j\setminus T|\le nj\le nL$. Below the cap, the parent of each maximal square is mixed. Equation <a href="#scanner:mixed-piece" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:mixed-piece">[scanner:mixed-piece]</a> therefore bounds the number of squares of side $u$ by $C(N_0+n/u)\le Cn/u$, since $u\le L\le s_0$ and $N_0s_0\le n$. All these squares are safe: their sites lie in $T_j$, their sides are at most $s_0$, and $$\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(T_j,Z)\ge\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(T,Z)-j
   >4D_0s_0-s_0>D_0s_0.$$ Subadditivity and the assumed box bound now give $$S_\Omega(Q_j)
 \le C_e n\sum_{\substack{u\le L\\u\ \mathrm{dyadic}}}u^e
 \le C'_e nL^e.$$ Covering $T$ in the same way, with cap comparable to $s_0$, uses $O(n/s_0)$ squares at the cap and $O(n/u)$ below it, and gives the first bound in <a href="#scanner:template-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:template-entropy">[scanner:template-entropy]</a>.

Adding an arbitrary part of one depth row changes entropy by at most $n\log q$. Finally, near these sets there is no edge joining $A$ to its complement: such an edge would have an endpoint in $Z$ within distance $s_0+1$ of $T$. Thus their physical boundaries are bounded by the ambient template and shell boundaries just counted. This argument does not count missing lattice edges as physical boundary edges. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-54"></a>
#### A small safe-box exponent

We use the scanner first with a bounded total metric weight. The rough comparison is sufficient here, even when $a\sqrt{\mathcal B}$ is large. This separates the bootstrap from the sharper concentration condition needed only in the final application.

<a id="stmt-prop-small-box"></a>
<div id="prop:small-box" class="proposition">

**Proposition 29** (Improved safe-box estimate). *There is a constant $C$, depending only on the Hamiltonian parameters, such that $$F_{\rm box}(r)\le Cr^{1+e_*}\quad(r\ge1),
 \qquad e_*=2\cdot10^{-6}.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-small-box"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-small-box</summary>

<a id="scanner:bootstrap-parameters"></a>
*Proof.* Let $e_0\in(0,1)$ be supplied by Proposition <a href="#prop:initial-box" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:initial-box">7</a>. If $e_0\le e_*$, the assertion already follows. Otherwise fix, once for the entire bootstrap, $$g_0=(1-e_0)/2,
 \quad \mu=1-g_0,
 \quad \nu=g_0/1000,
 \quad \ell=\nu/100,
 \quad \kappa=\min(\nu/100,e_*/4),
 \quad W=4.
 \label{scanner:bootstrap-parameters}$$ These parameters will not change when the current entropy exponent improves.

Suppose $F_{\rm box}(r)\le C_e r^{1+e}$, where $e_*<e\le e_0$. Take any safe integer rectangle $T$ of actual maximal side length $s_0$, and set $n=\lceil C_2s_0\rceil$ for a sufficiently large fixed $C_2$. If $A\cap T$ is empty, its entropy is zero, so assume otherwise. For large $s_0$, $L=o(s_0)$, so <a href="#scanner:test-geometry" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:test-geometry">[scanner:test-geometry]</a> holds. In particular the weaker safe-box clearance $D_0s_0$, rather than the stronger template clearance of Definition <a href="#scanner:template" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:template">27</a>, is enough for this application.

Here is the shell entropy input explicitly. The shell $T_j\setminus T$, $j\le L$, has area $O(nL)$ and consists of a bounded number of rectangular strips. Its mixed dyadic squares of side $u$ number $O(n/u+1)$, by the boundary-line count. The maximal-contained-square argument of Lemma <a href="#scanner:templates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:templates">28</a>, capped at side comparable to $L$, therefore gives $S_\Omega(Q_j)\le C_e nL^e$. These covering squares are safe: their sides are at most $L$, and their distance from $Z$ is at least $D_0s_0-L>D_0L$ once $s_0$ is large. This also covers thin rectangles. The target entropy is at most $C_e s_0^{1+e}$. Adding a partial row costs $O(n)$, so all the hypotheses of Proposition <a href="#prop:scanner" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:scanner">26</a> hold.

<a id="scanner:bootstrap-energy"></a>
We check its quantitative output. Since $K\asymp n^{g_0-\ell}$, $a\asymp n^{-g_0+\ell}$. In <a href="#scanner:density-output" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:density-output">[scanner:density-output]</a> the two powers before logarithms are at most $$e_0-\mu+\nu=-0.999g_0,
 \qquad -(g_0-\ell)/4+\nu=-0.2489975g_0.$$ Thus $\delta_n\le n^{-0.24g_0}$ for sufficiently large $n$, after constants and fixed logarithmic powers have been absorbed. The energy prefactor has power $\ell+2\kappa\le0.00003g_0$. Its slower decaying input is $\epsilon=n^{-0.001g_0}$, rather than $\delta_n^{1/8}\le n^{-0.03g_0}$. Hence $$E_{{\rm def},k}\le Cn^{-\nu/2}+o_k(1).
 \label{scanner:bootstrap-energy}$$ All scale conditions and the smallness of $ar_0^2$ hold at large $n$. No sharp marginal-moment condition has been used.

<a id="scanner:bootstrap-comparison"></a>
Put $\tau=n^{-\nu/4}$. Apply the rough upper and lower comparisons <a href="#comparator:rough-upper" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="comparator:rough-upper">[comparator:rough-upper]</a> and <a href="#comparator:rough-lower" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="comparator:rough-lower">[comparator:rough-lower]</a> at the selected interpolation. Write $S_X=S_{\widetilde\Omega}(X)$. The upper pin cost has leading coefficient $2S_X$; the lower coefficient is $4sWS_X=4S_X$. Replacing $\log d_*$ and $S'$ by $S_X$ costs $O(w+|\log z|)$. The remaining relative loss in this coefficient is at most $C(\tau+E_{{\rm def},k}/\tau)$, which is small after taking $k\to\infty$ and then $n$ sufficiently large. The two comparisons consequently imply $$S_X\le C_e\bigl(nL^e+nD+w+h(\tau)/a+1\bigr).
 \label{scanner:bootstrap-comparison}$$ To justify the order of limits in this absorption, keep $n$ fixed in both norm comparisons and use <a href="#scanner:bootstrap-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:bootstrap-energy">[scanner:bootstrap-energy]</a>. The resulting scalar inequality has the same $S_X$ for every $k$; all other remainders are uniform at the selected points and vanish. Only then choose the large-scale threshold making the coefficient loss smaller than the fixed margin between four and two.

For $0<\tau<1/2$, $h(\tau)\le C\tau\log(e/\tau)$. Therefore $$h(\tau)/a
 \le C n^{g_0-\ell-\nu/4}\log n=O(n),$$ because $g_0<1/2$. Also $w=n^{3/5}\le n$, and $\kappa\le e_*/4<(1-\ell)e$ while $e>e_*$. Equation <a href="#scanner:bootstrap-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:bootstrap-comparison">[scanner:bootstrap-comparison]</a>, followed by the negligible transfer back to $\Omega$, gives $$S_\Omega(A\cap T)\le C'_e n^{1+(1-\ell)e}
                       \le C''_e s_0^{1+(1-\ell)e}.$$ Bounded $s_0$ are included by increasing the constant, using the volume bound. Taking the supremum over safe boxes thus replaces the current exponent $e$ by $(1-\ell)e$.

Starting from $e_0$, finitely many repetitions reach an exponent at most $e_*$, which can be loosened to $e_*$. Every iteration uses only the current safe-box estimate on the shell covering squares. The parameters in <a href="#scanner:bootstrap-parameters" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:bootstrap-parameters">[scanner:bootstrap-parameters]</a>, and the finite number of iterations, depend only on the fixed Hamiltonian parameters. Thus the final constant is uniform over the domain and cut. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-55"></a>
#### The collar mutual information

After the bootstrap we allow the total metric weight to grow slowly. The exact norm comparison then charges the remaining target pin cost by the reciprocal of that weight. This is the point at which the entropy identity in Proposition <a href="#prop:comparators" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:comparators">24</a> gives a bound independent of the selected history.

<a id="stmt-prop-collar"></a>
<div id="prop:collar" class="proposition">

<a id="scanner:collar-output"></a>
**Proposition 30** (A sublinear collar bound). *Let $T$ be a template separated from the cut, with parameters $(n,s_0)$ as in Definition <a href="#scanner:template" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:template">27</a>. Set $$L=\lfloor n^{1-10^{-5}}\rfloor,
 \qquad X=A\cap T,
 \qquad S_0=A\cap T_L,$$ and suppose $L\le s_0$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $$I_\Omega(X:\Lambda\setminus S_0)
       \le C n^{1-\varepsilon},\qquad \varepsilon=10^{-5}.
 \label{scanner:collar-output}$$ The constant and threshold are independent of $T,s_0,n,\Lambda$, and $A$. The cuts of $X,S_0$, and $S_0\setminus X$ have $O(n)$ edges, and $|S_0|=O(n^2)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-collar"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-collar</summary>

*Proof.* If $X$ is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise Proposition <a href="#prop:small-box" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:small-box">29</a> and Lemma <a href="#scanner:templates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:templates">28</a> supply <a href="#scanner:entropy-input" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:entropy-input">[scanner:entropy-input]</a> with $e=e_*=2\cdot10^{-6}$. Since $s_0\le n$, the core entropy is at most $Cn^{1+e}$. The template clearance and $L\le s_0$ imply <a href="#scanner:test-geometry" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:test-geometry">[scanner:test-geometry]</a> at large $n$; the logarithmic truncation radius is negligible compared with $L$.

<a id="scanner:final-energy"></a>
Use the following fixed parameter choices: <a id="scanner:final-parameters"></a>$$\mu=\frac14,\quad \nu=\frac1{1000},\quad
 \ell=\frac1{100000},\quad
 \omega=\frac1{20000},\quad
 \kappa=\frac1{1000000},\quad W=n^\omega.
 \label{scanner:final-parameters}$$ Then $a\asymp n^{-0.74994}$. The two terms in <a href="#scanner:density-output" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:density-output">[scanner:density-output]</a> have powers $-0.248998$ and $-0.186485$, before the fixed logarithmic factors. Hence $\delta_n\le n^{-0.18}$ at sufficiently large scales. The power of the energy prefactor is $$\ell+2\kappa+2\omega=0.000112.$$ The $\epsilon=n^{-0.001}$ term is again the limiting one, and Proposition <a href="#prop:scanner" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:scanner">26</a> gives $$E_{{\rm def},k}\le Cn^{-0.0005}+o_k(1).
 \label{scanner:final-energy}$$ Set $\tau=n^{-0.00025}$. All fixed multiples of $a$ lie in the marginal-moment interval required for the sharp comparisons, since $$a\sqrt{\mathcal B}
 \le C n^{-0.2499395}(\log n)^C\longrightarrow0.$$

At each leaf write, as before, the physical partition as $X,U,Y,V$. All entropies in the next calculation refer to $\widetilde\Omega$. Let $$g_{\rm pre}=S(XU)+S(V)-S(Y),\qquad
 g_{\rm post}=S(U)+S(UY)-S(Y).$$ These are the quantities in the sharp norm comparisons. Their upper bounds are uniform in the status. In particular $S(XU)\le S(X)+S(U)\le Cn^{1+e}$, and by purity $S(V)=S(XUY)\le S(X)+S(UY)\le Cn^{1+e}$. Here the matched-prefix error $CnD$ is absorbed because $\kappa<e$. Thus $0\le g_{\rm pre}\le Cn^{1+e}$.

<a id="scanner:final-errors"></a>
Denote the full terminal path and uniform band average by $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rm leaf}$. Subtracting <a href="#comparator:sharp-upper" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="comparator:sharp-upper">[comparator:sharp-upper]</a> from <a href="#comparator:sharp-lower" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="comparator:sharp-lower">[comparator:sharp-lower]</a>, and then dividing by $2sW$, bounds $2S(X)+\langle g_{\rm pre}-g_{\rm post}\rangle_{\rm leaf}$ by a constant times $$\frac{S(X)+1}{W}+w
 +(\tau+E_{{\rm def},k}/\tau)n^{1+e}
 +\frac{h(\tau)}a+a\mathcal B
 +\frac{|\log z|}a+o_k(1).
 \label{scanner:final-errors}$$ This calculation uses $S'=S(X)+O(w+|\log z|)$ and the analogous estimate for $\log d_*$. It also restores the lost $\tau\langle g_{\rm pre}\rangle_{\rm leaf}$ from the lower comparison using the preceding uniform bound.

<a id="scanner:entropy-identity"></a>
For each leaf separately, purity gives the exact identity $$2S(X)+g_{\rm pre}-g_{\rm post}
       =I(X:V)+I(X:YV).
 \label{scanner:entropy-identity}$$ Both $V$ and $YV$ contain the fixed subsystem $\Lambda\setminus S_0$. Monotonicity of mutual information therefore makes the left side of <a href="#scanner:entropy-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:entropy-identity">[scanner:entropy-identity]</a> at least $I_{\widetilde\Omega}(X:\Lambda\setminus S_0)$, independently of the history. This remains true after the leaf average, even though the selected round and its weights can vary with $k$.

For completeness, after $k\to\infty$ the terms in <a href="#scanner:final-errors" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:final-errors">[scanner:final-errors]</a> have the following upper bounds on their powers of $n$, apart from fixed logarithms.

<div class="center">

| Error term                                               | Power of $n$ |
|:---------------------------------------------------------|:------------:|
| $(S(X)+1)/W$                                             |  $0.999952$  |
| $w$                                                      |    $0.6$     |
| $(\tau+E_{{\rm def},k}/\tau)n^{1+e}$, after $k\to\infty$ |  $0.999752$  |
| $h(\tau)/a$                                              |  $0.74969$   |
| $a\mathcal B$                                            |  $0.250061$  |
| $|\log z|/a$                                             | $-99.25006$  |

</div>

All are strictly below $1-\varepsilon=0.99999$. Equation <a href="#scanner:final-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:final-energy">[scanner:final-energy]</a> controls the mass-loss term uniformly before the limit. This proves $I_{\widetilde\Omega}(X:\Lambda\setminus S_0)
\le Cn^{1-\varepsilon}$.

Finally write mutual information as $S(X)-S(X\mid\Lambda\setminus S_0)$ and use Lemma <a href="#lem:continuity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:continuity">3</a>. Only $\log\dim\mathcal H_X=O(n^2)$ enters, even if the far subsystem is very large. The trace distance $O(n^{-500})$ between the original and truncated ground states therefore changes this mutual information by $O(n^{-248})$. This proves <a href="#scanner:collar-output" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="scanner:collar-output">[scanner:collar-output]</a>. The final size and boundary assertions were established in Lemma <a href="#scanner:templates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:templates">28</a>. ◻

</details>

The replica construction has now been eliminated: the conclusion of Proposition <a href="#prop:collar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:collar">30</a> is an inequality for the original finite ground state. The next section applies the exact positive quasi-local system to that state. In particular, the exponentially large auxiliary operator used there never multiplies a truncation or a replica error from the present argument.

<a id="sec:amplification"></a>
### Amplifying the collar estimate

Proposition <a href="#prop:collar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:collar">30</a> gives a sublinear bound on the mutual information between a target and the region beyond its collar. We now make this mutual information smaller than any fixed inverse power of the scale, at the cost of a slightly wider collar. Typical spectral subspaces first give a candidate restoring operator whose norm is controlled by the collar mutual information. Positive constraints suppress its excited component, yielding accurate restoration after localization. A polar decomposition then replaces this operator by a local unitary. An untouched reference copy records the target’s correlations with the remote system and witnesses their decoupling.

<a id="eq:amplification-exponents"></a>
<a id="eq:amplification-positive-system"></a>
Throughout this section fix $$\label{eq:amplification-exponents}
 \varepsilon=10^{-5},\qquad \beta=1-2\cdot10^{-6},\qquad
 \alpha=\frac{p}{p+1}>1-10^{-6},$$ where the integer $p$ is fixed. Apply Proposition <a href="#prop:positive" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:positive">10</a> with this value of $p$. Thus, in this section, $H_F=\sum_i k_i$ is a fresh exact positive system with $$\label{eq:amplification-positive-system}
 0\le k_i\le I,\quad k_i\Omega=0,\quad
 H_F\ge g(I-P_\Omega),\qquad
 P_\Omega=|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|,$$ and $g>0$ is independent of the finite domain. The scanner’s truncated Hamiltonian is no longer used. All neighborhoods below are neighborhoods in the induced graph: for $S\subseteq\Lambda$ we write $N_r(S)=\{y\in\Lambda:d_\Lambda(y,S)\le r\}=N_r^\Lambda(S)$.

<a id="pm-h-57"></a>
#### Localizing products of positive constraints

The following estimate supplies the localization needed later. It is stated for a general operator, which may act on additional finite systems. These additional systems are spectators in the dynamics. The spatial truncation argument has the propagation structure of dissipative Lieb–Robinson estimates (Barthel and Kliesch 2012, Theorems 1 and 2) <a id="pm-cite-54"></a>[[BarthelKliesch2012](#ref-BarthelKliesch2012)]. We prove it here on coupled clock realizations, since the needed bound is an expectation of a norm.

<a id="stmt-lem-amplification-local-products"></a>
<div id="lem:amplification-local-products" class="lemma">

**Lemma 31** (Local constraint products). *Let positive contractions $k_i$, anchored at $a_i\in\Lambda$ with bounded multiplicity, satisfy $$\|k_i-E_{i,l}k_i\|\le C e^{-c l^\alpha}\qquad(l\ge0),$$ where $E_{i,l}$ is conditional expectation onto $N_l(a_i)$. Set $G_i=(I-k_i)^{1/2}$ and $K_i=k_i^{1/2}$. Fix $t\ge0$ and an integer $r\ge1$. At each anchor label run an independent rate-one Poisson clock on $[0,t]$. In occurrence order, with later factors on the left, let $D$ be the product of all $G_i$, and let $D_{\rm ret}$ retain only events with $d_\Lambda(a_i,S)\le r$, for a nonempty set $S\subseteq\Lambda$. Let $L$ be the same retained product with each $G_i$ replaced by $G_{i,r}=(I-E_{i,r}k_i)^{1/2}$.*

<a id="eq:amplification-product-truncation"></a>
<a id="eq:amplification-product-omission"></a>
*There are uniform constants $C,c,v>0$ such that $$\label{eq:amplification-product-truncation}
 \mathbb E\|D_{\rm ret}-L\|
 \le Ct|S|(1+r)^2e^{-c r^\alpha}.$$ In particular $L$ is a contraction supported on $N_{2r}(S)$. If $k_i\Omega=0$ and an operator $B$ is supported on $S$ and spectator systems, then, for every unit spectator vector $\xi$, $$\label{eq:amplification-product-omission}
 \mathbb E\|(D-D_{\rm ret})B(\Omega\otimes\xi)\|
 \le Ct|S|\|B\|e^{vt-c r^\alpha}.$$ Both bounds concern the same coupled clock realization. Their constants are independent of $|\Lambda|$ and of spectator dimensions.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-amplification-local-products"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-amplification-local-products</summary>

<a id="eq:amplification-channel-vector"></a>
*Proof.* We first prove an operator estimate for unital channels. Define $$\mathcal E_i(B)=G_iBG_i+K_iBK_i,
 \qquad
 \mathcal E_{i,l}(B)=G_{i,l}BG_{i,l}+K_{i,l}BK_{i,l},$$ where $K_{i,l}=(E_{i,l}k_i)^{1/2}$. When $k_i\Omega=0$, functional calculus gives $G_i\Omega=\Omega$ and $K_i\Omega=0$, so $$\label{eq:amplification-channel-vector}
 \mathcal E_i(C)(\Omega\otimes\xi)=G_iC(\Omega\otimes\xi)$$ for every operator $C$ and spectator vector $\xi$. Products of these channels therefore recover the contraction products when evaluated on the ground vector. We localize the channels first: their unitality makes each local channel fix the algebra outside its supporting ball. They are also completely positive, hence contractions in operator norm, including after adjoining spectators. Lemma <a href="#lem:quasilocal-roots" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:quasilocal-roots">11</a> gives <a id="eq:amplification-channel-approximation"></a>$$\label{eq:amplification-channel-approximation}
 \|\mathcal E_i-\mathcal E_{i,l}\|_{\rm cb}
 \le C e^{-c l^\alpha}.$$ The completely bounded norm here is the supremum of the operator norms after adjoining identity maps on finite spectator systems. In this case the estimate follows directly from the norm bounds for the two square roots, so it has no dimension factor.

<a id="eq:amplification-shell-oscillation"></a>
Put $\mathcal E_{i,-1}=\mathop{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\Delta_{i,l}=\mathcal E_{i,l}-\mathcal E_{i,l-1}$ for $l\ge0$. By increasing $C$ to include $l=0$, <a id="eq:amplification-channel-shells"></a>$$\label{eq:amplification-channel-shells}
 \|\Delta_{i,l}\|_{\rm cb}\le C e^{-c l^\alpha}.$$ Both channels in this difference fix operators commuting with the algebra on $N_l(a_i)$. Thus the difference vanishes on that commutant. For an operator $B$ define its oscillation at a physical site $y$ by $$d_y(B)=\sup_{U_y\ {\rm unitary}}\|[U_y,B]\|.$$ Average over the on-site unitaries in a set $Q$, one site at a time. The total norm change is at most $\sum_{z\in Q}d_z(B)$, and the result commutes with the algebra on $Q$. Consequently $$\label{eq:amplification-shell-oscillation}
 \|\Delta_{i,l}(B)\|
 \le C e^{-c l^\alpha}\sum_{z\in N_l(a_i)}d_z(B).$$ This argument also applies to operators acting on spectators.

<a id="eq:amplification-oscillation-increment"></a>
To bound the oscillation after one event, suppose first that $m=d_\Lambda(a_i,y)<\infty$. The channel $\mathcal E_{i,m-1}$ does not act at $y$ and commutes with conjugation by $U_y$; hence it cannot increase $d_y$. Telescope the shells from radius $m$ onward and use $d_y(C)\le2\|C\|$ to obtain $$\label{eq:amplification-oscillation-increment}
 d_y(\mathcal E_i B)\le d_y(B)+
 C\sum_{l\ge d_\Lambda(a_i,y)}e^{-c l^\alpha}
       \sum_{z\in N_l(a_i)}d_z(B).$$ For $m=0$ the initial channel is the identity. If $m=\infty$, $\mathcal E_i$ acts in a different component and cannot increase $d_y$. Exact component support follows either from the construction or by letting $l$ exceed the component diameter in the approximation assumption.

<a id="eq:amplification-weighted-kernel"></a>
Sum the increment in <a href="#eq:amplification-oscillation-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-oscillation-increment">[eq:amplification-oscillation-increment]</a> over the retained anchor labels. Define the nonnegative matrix $$A_{yz}=C\sum_{i\ {\rm retained}}\sum_{l\ge0}
 e^{-cl^\alpha}\mathbf1_{\{y,z\in N_l(a_i)\}},$$ with the constant from <a href="#eq:amplification-oscillation-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-oscillation-increment">[eq:amplification-oscillation-increment]</a>. It has a uniformly bounded weighted row sum: $$\label{eq:amplification-weighted-kernel}
 \sup_y\sum_{z:\,d_\Lambda(y,z)<\infty}
 A_{yz}e^{a d_\Lambda(y,z)^\alpha}\le v$$ for some $a>0$. Indeed, at radius $l$ there are at most $C(1+l)^2$ anchor labels whose balls contain $y$, and at most $C(1+l)^2$ sites in each ball. Their distances from $y$ are at most $2l$. The left side is therefore bounded by $$C\sum_{l\ge0}(1+l)^4e^{-c l^\alpha+a(2l)^\alpha},$$ which is finite for sufficiently small $a$. There are no kernel entries between different components.

<a id="eq:amplification-propagation"></a>
Let $B_u$ be the result of the retained channel events up to time $u$, starting from $B$. The Poisson jump formula and <a href="#eq:amplification-oscillation-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-oscillation-increment">[eq:amplification-oscillation-increment]</a> imply, in integral form, the differential upper bound $$\frac{d}{du}\mathbb E d_y(B_u)
 \le\sum_z A_{yz}\mathbb E d_z(B_u).$$ The site and anchor sums are finite for a fixed domain, and the radius sums converge absolutely with the uniform bounds in <a href="#eq:amplification-weighted-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-weighted-kernel">[eq:amplification-weighted-kernel]</a>. Initially $d_y(B)\le2\|B\|1_S(y)$. On components meeting $S$, weight the last inequality by $e^{a d_\Lambda(y,S)^\alpha}$. The triangle inequality and $0<\alpha<1$ give $$d_\Lambda(y,S)^\alpha-d_\Lambda(z,S)^\alpha
 \le d_\Lambda(y,z)^\alpha.$$ The weighted supremum thus grows at rate at most $v$. Gronwall’s inequality yields $$\label{eq:amplification-propagation}
 \mathbb E d_y(B_u)
 \le2\|B\|e^{vu-a d_\Lambda(y,S)^\alpha}.$$ Oscillations on components disjoint from $S$ remain zero.

<a id="eq:amplification-omitted-event"></a>
We can now remove the distant events. For an omitted anchor at finite distance $d=d_\Lambda(a_i,S)>r$, sum <a href="#eq:amplification-shell-oscillation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-shell-oscillation">[eq:amplification-shell-oscillation]</a> over all $l\ge0$ and apply <a href="#eq:amplification-propagation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-propagation">[eq:amplification-propagation]</a>. When $l\le d/2$, every $z\in N_l(a_i)$ has $d_\Lambda(z,S)\ge d/2$. The sum over these radii is bounded by $C\|B\|e^{vu-a(d/2)^\alpha}$. For $l>d/2$ use the shell decay and the ball cardinality instead. Absorbing its polynomial factor gives, in both cases, $$\label{eq:amplification-omitted-event}
 \mathbb E\|(\mathcal E_i-\mathop{\mathrm{id}})(B_u)\|
 \le C\|B\|e^{vu-c'd^\alpha}.$$ At infinite distance the left side is zero.

<a id="eq:amplification-channel-omission"></a>
Couple full and retained processes by using the same clocks. The difference of their products telescopes with earlier retained channels and later full channels. All the later channels contract the operator norm. The earlier retained process is independent of the omitted clocks, so their expected contributions are obtained by integrating the rate-one bound <a href="#eq:amplification-omitted-event" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-omitted-event">[eq:amplification-omitted-event]</a>. There are at most $C|S|(d+1)^2$ anchor labels at distance $d$ from $S$. Summing the stretched-exponential tail and integrating time therefore prove the coupled expected-norm estimate $$\label{eq:amplification-channel-omission}
 \mathbb E\|\mathcal E_{\rm full}(B)-\mathcal E_{\rm ret}(B)\|
 \le Ct|S|\|B\|e^{vt-c''r^\alpha}.$$ In particular this is a bound on the expectation of the norm, not merely on the norm of a difference of averaged operators.

If $k_i\Omega=0$, evaluating both channel products on $\Omega\otimes\xi$ and iterating <a href="#eq:amplification-channel-vector" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-channel-vector">[eq:amplification-channel-vector]</a> converts <a href="#eq:amplification-channel-omission" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-channel-omission">[eq:amplification-channel-omission]</a> into <a href="#eq:amplification-product-omission" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-product-omission">[eq:amplification-product-omission]</a>. Unitality is essential in the channel argument: the single map $C\mapsto G_iCG_i$ need not fix operators on a disjoint system.

Finally there are at most $C|S|(1+r)^2$ retained labels, and hence their expected number of events is at most $Ct|S|(1+r)^2$. Each event’s contraction changes by at most $Ce^{-c r^\alpha}$ under radius-$r$ approximation. Telescoping the contraction products proves <a href="#eq:amplification-product-truncation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-product-truncation">[eq:amplification-product-truncation]</a>. A retained anchor is within $r$ of $S$, so every approximating factor is supported on $N_{2r}(S)$. This completes the proof. ◻

</details>

<a id="eq:amplification-excited-decay"></a>
Ground-state-preserving products that suppress excited states also occur in detectability-lemma constructions (Anshu, Arad, and Vidick 2016, sec. III) <a id="pm-cite-55"></a>[[AnshuAradVidick2016](#ref-AnshuAradVidick2016)]. For the random contractions here, the gap gives the following estimate. Under <a href="#eq:amplification-positive-system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-positive-system">[eq:amplification-positive-system]</a>, for any vector $\zeta$ including spectator systems, $$\label{eq:amplification-excited-decay}
 \mathbb E\|D(I-P_\Omega)\zeta\|^2
 \le e^{-gt}\|(I-P_\Omega)\zeta\|^2.$$ Here and below physical projections are tensored with the identity on spectators. To see this, every self-adjoint $G_i$ fixes $\Omega$ and commutes with $P_\Omega$. At a clock event the squared norm of an excited vector decreases by $\langle\zeta,k_i\zeta\rangle$. Summing the conditional rate of these decreases gives at least $g\|\zeta\|^2$, and integrating proves <a href="#eq:amplification-excited-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-excited-decay">[eq:amplification-excited-decay]</a>. Thus the global gap is used for decay, while the preceding channel argument supplies locality.

<a id="pm-h-58"></a>
#### A local unitary from a small collar cost

For an ambient set $T\subset\mathbb Z^2$, write $T_L=T+[-L,L]^2_{\mathbb Z}$ as in the scanner. The next proposition states explicitly the information it needs from that scanner.

<a id="stmt-prop-amplification"></a>
<div id="prop:amplification" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:amplification-input-information"></a>
<a id="eq:amplification-radius"></a>
<a id="eq:amplification-output"></a>
**Proposition 32** (Amplification). *Fix $C_0>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\beta,\alpha$ be as in <a href="#eq:amplification-exponents" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-exponents">[eq:amplification-exponents]</a>. Suppose $n\ge2$, $L=\lfloor n^{1-\varepsilon}\rfloor$, and $$X=A\cap T,\qquad S_0=A\cap T_L,\qquad Y=S_0\setminus X,
 \qquad Z'=\Lambda\setminus S_0.$$ Assume that $|S_0|\le C_0n^2$, that each of the three cuts $X,Y,S_0$ has at most $C_0n$ crossing edges, and that $$\label{eq:amplification-input-information}
 \mathcal I:=I_\Omega(X:Z')\le C_0n^{1-\varepsilon}.$$ For every integer $M\ge1$, at all sufficiently large $n$, there is an integer radius $r$ such that $$\label{eq:amplification-radius}
 r\le C_M n^{(1-\varepsilon)/\alpha},\qquad
 L+2r=o(n^\beta),$$ and, simultaneously for every physical set $J\subseteq\Lambda\setminus N_{2r}(S_0)$, $$\label{eq:amplification-output}
 I_\Omega(X:J)\le C_M n^{-M}.$$ The same bound holds with any subset of $X$ in place of $X$. The constants and the threshold may depend on $C_0$ and $M$, but are independent of $\Lambda,A,T$ subject to the stated assumptions.*

<a id="eq:amplification-cut-clearance"></a>
*If in addition $$\label{eq:amplification-cut-clearance}
 \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(T,Z)>L+n^\beta,$$ where $Z$ is the set of endpoints of the original cut, then $N_{2r}(S_0)\subseteq A$. In particular the remote set $J$ may include all of $\Lambda\setminus A$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-amplification"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-amplification</summary>

*Proof.* The case $X=\varnothing$ is immediate; take $r=1$. Suppose that $X$ is nonempty. We keep the entire physical system fixed while constructing the auxiliary operators; the estimates below are uniform in its volume.

<a id="eq:amplification-typical-error"></a>
Set $w=n^{3/5}$. Lemma <a href="#lem:tail" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:tail">5</a>, applied in the original ground state to the three cuts, provides spectral projections $P_X,T_Y,Q_{S_0}$ onto their positive eigenvalues with surprisal in the intervals $$[S(X)-w,S(X)+w],\quad [S(Y)-w,S(Y)+w],\quad
 [S(S_0)-w,S(S_0)+w],$$ respectively. The original interactions have uniformly bounded support dimensions and at most $Cn$ terms cross each cut. Thus each failed projection has probability at most $C\exp(-cn^{1/10})$. For any fixed integer $K\ge1$, increasing the scale threshold makes these three probabilities at most $$\label{eq:amplification-typical-error}
 \delta=n^{-2K}.$$ For a trivial subsystem its projection is the identity. All inverse eigenvalues used below are restricted to the selected positive spectrum, so no invertibility assumption is imposed on a marginal.

<a id="eq:amplification-restored-state"></a>
Choose a full eigenbasis $\{|x\rangle\}$ for $\rho_X$, with eigenvalues $p_x\ge0$, and write a Schmidt expansion $$\Omega=\sum_{y:\,p_y>0}\sqrt{p_y}\,
 |y\rangle_X|\omega_y\rangle_{YZ'}.$$ Append two systems $s',e'$, each a copy of the Hilbert space on $X$, with fixed unit blank vectors denoted $|0\rangle$. Consider the unit vectors <a id="eq:amplification-swapped-state"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \phi&=|0\rangle_X|0\rangle_{s'}
       \sum_{y:\,p_y>0}\sqrt{p_y}|y\rangle_{e'}
                                    |\omega_y\rangle_{YZ'},
       \label{eq:amplification-swapped-state}\\
 \eta&=\Omega\otimes
       \sum_{x:\,p_x>0}\sqrt{p_x}|x\rangle_{s'}|x\rangle_{e'}.
       \label{eq:amplification-restored-state}
\end{aligned}$$ In $\phi$, the original target has moved to $e'$, so its joint reduction with a remote physical system is unchanged after relabeling. In $\eta$, $e'$ is purified by $s'$ and is independent of all physical systems. The unitary we construct will leave $e'$ untouched and act only on $s'$ and a graph neighborhood of $S_0$.

<a id="eq:amplification-restoring-operator"></a>
<a id="eq:amplification-column-identity"></a>
For readability write $Q=Q_{S_0}$ and $T_0=T_Y$. On $s',X,Y$ define the square operator $$\label{eq:amplification-restoring-operator}
 R_0=\sum_{x\ {\rm selected}}p_x^{-1/2}
 |x\rangle\langle0|_{s'}\otimes
 Q\bigl(|x\rangle\langle0|_X\otimes T_0\bigr).$$ It acts trivially on $e'$ and $Z'$. The localization lemma applies to vectors of the form $B(\Omega\otimes\xi)$ with a local operator $B$. To put $R_0\phi$ in this form, define an operator supported on $S_0,s',e'$ by <a id="eq:amplification-column-operator"></a>$$\label{eq:amplification-column-operator}
 B_0=\sum_{\substack{x\ {\rm selected}\\y\ {\rm in\ the\ full\ basis}}}
 p_x^{-1/2}|x\rangle\langle0|_{s'}\otimes
 |y\rangle\langle0|_{e'}\otimes
 Q\bigl(|x\rangle\langle y|_X\otimes T_0\bigr).$$ The summation over $y$ includes zero-probability eigenvectors. Direct substitution gives $$\label{eq:amplification-column-identity}
 R_0\phi=B_0(\Omega\otimes|00\rangle_{s'e'}).$$

<a id="eq:amplification-operator-norm"></a>
We establish three estimates for these operators before introducing the constraint product. The first is a norm bound controlled by $\mathcal I$. Let $$B_Y=\sum_{x\ {\rm selected}}p_x^{-1}
       T_0\langle x|Q|x\rangle T_0\ge0.$$ Orthogonality of the output vectors in <a href="#eq:amplification-restoring-operator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-restoring-operator">[eq:amplification-restoring-operator]</a> gives $R_0^\dagger R_0=|0\rangle\langle0|_{s'}\otimes
|0\rangle\langle0|_X\otimes B_Y$. Similarly, $B_0^\dagger B_0=|00\rangle\langle00|_{s'e'}\otimes
I_X\otimes B_Y$. The typical spectral inequalities are $$p_x^{-1}\le e^{S(X)+w},\qquad
 Q\le e^{S(S_0)+w}\rho_{S_0},\qquad
 T_0\rho_Y T_0\le e^{-S(Y)+w}T_0.$$ They imply $$\label{eq:amplification-operator-norm}
 \|R_0\|,\ \|B_0\|\le M_0,\qquad
 M_0=\exp\bigl((\mathcal I+3w)/2\bigr),$$ because purity gives $S(X)+S(S_0)-S(Y)=I(X:Z')=\mathcal I$.

<a id="eq:amplification-adjoint-error"></a>
The second estimate is an adjoint identity with no factor $M_0$. Let $\mathcal R_X$ be the isometry that relabels $X$ as $e'$ and inserts the blank vectors on $X,s'$; thus $\mathcal R_X\Omega=\phi$. For every physical operator $L'$ the coefficients $\sqrt{p_x}$ in <a href="#eq:amplification-restored-state" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-restored-state">[eq:amplification-restored-state]</a> cancel the selected inverse square roots, giving exactly <a id="eq:amplification-adjoint-identity"></a>$$\label{eq:amplification-adjoint-identity}
 R_0^\dagger (L')^\dagger\eta
 =\mathcal R_X(P_X\otimes T_0)Q(L')^\dagger\Omega.$$ The three projections are contractions, whether or not they commute. Telescoping them on $\Omega$ and using <a href="#eq:amplification-typical-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-typical-error">[eq:amplification-typical-error]</a> therefore gives $$\label{eq:amplification-adjoint-error}
 \|R_0^\dagger(L')^\dagger\eta-\phi\|
 \le3\sqrt\delta+\|(L')^\dagger\Omega-\Omega\|.$$

<a id="eq:amplification-ground-component"></a>
Third, although $R_0\phi$ may have large norm, its physical ground component has norm at most one. Define $$M_X=\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}_Y\bigl[(I_X\otimes T_0)\rho_{S_0}Q\bigr].$$ Since $Q$ commutes with $\rho_{S_0}$, one has $0\le\rho_{S_0}Q\le\rho_{S_0}$. Cyclicity of the partial trace for operators on $Y$ allows a second $T_0$ on the right. Hence $$0\le M_X\le\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}_Y[(I\otimes T_0)\rho_{S_0}(I\otimes T_0)]
 \le\rho_X.$$ The last inequality follows by adding the analogous positive term with $I-T_0$; the two cross terms have zero partial trace. In particular $M_X$ vanishes on $\ker\rho_X$. On its support put $A_X=\rho_X^{-1/2}M_X\rho_X^{-1/2}$, so $0\le A_X\le I$. With $\rho_X^+$ denoting the inverse on the support and zero on the kernel, $$M_X\rho_X^+M_X
 =\rho_X^{1/2}A_X^2\rho_X^{1/2}\le M_X.$$ The ancillary coefficient of $|x\rangle_{s'}|y\rangle_{e'}$ in $P_\Omega R_0\phi$ is $(M_X)_{yx}/\sqrt{p_x}$ for selected $x$. It follows that $$\label{eq:amplification-ground-component}
 \|P_\Omega R_0\phi\|^2
 =\sum_{x\ {\rm selected},y}\frac{|(M_X)_{yx}|^2}{p_x}
 \le\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}(M_X\rho_X^+M_X)\le\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}M_X\le1.$$

We have now constructed a restoring operator whose norm is $e^{O(\mathcal I+w)}$, whose adjoint is accurate on the desired state, and whose ground component is bounded. Positive constraints will suppress the remaining component while preserving the last two properties.

<a id="eq:amplification-time-choice"></a>
Run the clocks of Lemma <a href="#lem:amplification-local-products" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:amplification-local-products">31</a> for time $$\label{eq:amplification-time-choice}
 t_*=C(\mathcal I+w+K\log n),\qquad
 r=\left\lceil\bigl(C'(t_*+K\log n)\bigr)^{1/\alpha}\right\rceil,$$ where $C$ and then $C'$ are chosen sufficiently large. Use $S=S_0$, and put $\zeta=R_0\phi$. The full, retained, and truncated products are denoted $D,D_{\rm ret},L'$ respectively. Equations <a href="#eq:amplification-excited-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-excited-decay">[eq:amplification-excited-decay]</a> and <a href="#eq:amplification-operator-norm" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-operator-norm">[eq:amplification-operator-norm]</a> imply $$\mathbb E\|D(I-P_\Omega)\zeta\|^2
 \le M_0^2e^{-gt_*}.$$ Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:amplification-local-products" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:amplification-local-products">31</a> with $B=B_0$, $\xi=|00\rangle_{s'e'}$, and $S=S_0$. The column representation <a href="#eq:amplification-column-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-column-identity">[eq:amplification-column-identity]</a> then gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\|(D-D_{\rm ret})\zeta\|
 &\le Ct_*|S_0|M_0e^{vt_*-cr^\alpha},\\
 M_0\mathbb E\|D_{\rm ret}-L'\|
 &\le Ct_*|S_0|(1+r)^2M_0e^{-cr^\alpha}.
\end{aligned}$$ All of these estimates are on the same clock space.

<a id="eq:amplification-good-trajectory"></a>
Here is explicit control of the scale choices. First choose $C$ so that $gt_*\ge\mathcal I+3w+6K\log n$. The first expectation is then at most $n^{-6K}$. By <a href="#eq:amplification-input-information" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-input-information">[eq:amplification-input-information]</a>, both $t_*$ and $r$ are bounded by fixed powers of $n$, with constants depending on $K$. Their polynomial prefactors and $|S_0|$ therefore cost only $O_K(\log n)$ in the logarithm. Since $\log M_0=(\mathcal I+3w)/2\le Ct_*$, choosing $C'$ larger makes each of the last two expectations at most $n^{-3K}$ for large $n$. Markov’s inequality and a union bound consequently provide a realization satisfying $$\label{eq:amplification-good-trajectory}
 \|D(I-P_\Omega)\zeta\|\le n^{-K},\quad
 \|(D-D_{\rm ret})\zeta\|\le n^{-K},\quad
 M_0\|D_{\rm ret}-L'\|\le n^{-K}.$$ Indeed the three failure probabilities sum to at most $n^{-4K}+2n^{-2K}<1$ at sufficiently large scales.

<a id="eq:amplification-before-polar"></a>
Every exact factor fixes the ground vector in both directions. Thus $D$ preserves the ground component in <a href="#eq:amplification-ground-component" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-ground-component">[eq:amplification-ground-component]</a>, and $D_{\rm ret}^\dagger\Omega=\Omega$. Since $M_0\ge1$, <a href="#eq:amplification-good-trajectory" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-good-trajectory">[eq:amplification-good-trajectory]</a> gives $$\label{eq:amplification-before-polar}
 \|L'R_0\phi\|\le1+3n^{-K},\qquad
 \|(L')^\dagger\Omega-\Omega\|\le n^{-K}.$$ Combining the latter bound with <a href="#eq:amplification-adjoint-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-adjoint-error">[eq:amplification-adjoint-error]</a>, and writing $R'=L'R_0$, we obtain $$\|(R')^\dagger\eta-\phi\|\le4n^{-K}.$$ Because $\phi,\eta$ are unit vectors, the real overlap satisfies $\Re\langle\eta,R'\phi\rangle\ge1-4n^{-K}$. Expanding the square using <a href="#eq:amplification-before-polar" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-before-polar">[eq:amplification-before-polar]</a> gives <a id="eq:amplification-direct-error"></a>$$\label{eq:amplification-direct-error}
 \|R'\phi-\eta\|\le Cn^{-K/2}.$$

<a id="eq:amplification-unitary-error"></a>
The square operator $R'$ is supported on $s'$ and $N_{2r}(S_0)$, and acts trivially on $e'$. Its polar decomposition extends on this finite local space to $R'=U'H_+$, where $U'$ is unitary and $H_+=(R'^\dagger R')^{1/2}$. Such a unitary extension exists even when $R'$ is singular: its two polar support spaces have equal dimension, as do their orthogonal complements. Tensor it with the identity elsewhere. For $\xi=(U')^\dagger\eta$ we have $$\|H_+\xi-\phi\|\le4n^{-K},\qquad
 \|H_+\phi-\xi\|\le Cn^{-K/2}.$$ Subtract these two errors in the identity $$(I+H_+)(\xi-\phi)
 =(H_+\xi-\phi)-(H_+\phi-\xi).$$ Since $\|(I+H_+)^{-1}\|\le1$, this proves $$\label{eq:amplification-unitary-error}
 \|U'\phi-\eta\|\le Cn^{-K/2}.$$ In particular no bound on $\|H_+\|$ is needed.

Let $J\subseteq\Lambda\setminus N_{2r}(S_0)$ be arbitrary. The unitary $U'$ changes neither $e'$ nor $J$, so their joint reduction in $U'\phi$ is exactly the original $XJ$ reduction, with $X$ relabeled as $e'$. In $\eta$ that joint reduction is a product. Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:continuity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:continuity">3</a> to $I(e':J)=S(e')-S(e'|J)$ and <a href="#eq:amplification-unitary-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-unitary-error">[eq:amplification-unitary-error]</a>. Only the dimension of $e'$ appears. It has $\log\dim e'=|X|\log q\le Cn^2$, and therefore $$I_\Omega(X:J)\le Cn^{2-K/4}.$$ Choose the fixed integer $K\ge4(M+3)$. This proves <a href="#eq:amplification-output" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-output">[eq:amplification-output]</a>, uniformly for every such $J$. Discarding part of $X$ proves the assertion for its subsets.

Finally <a href="#eq:amplification-time-choice" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-time-choice">[eq:amplification-time-choice]</a> and <a href="#eq:amplification-input-information" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-input-information">[eq:amplification-input-information]</a> give $r\le C_M n^{(1-\varepsilon)/\alpha}$. The choices in <a href="#eq:amplification-exponents" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-exponents">[eq:amplification-exponents]</a> imply $(1-\varepsilon)/\alpha<\beta$ and $1-\varepsilon<\beta$, which prove <a href="#eq:amplification-radius" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-radius">[eq:amplification-radius]</a>. If a graph path of length at most $2r$ from $S_0$ reached $\Lambda\setminus A$, it would contain an endpoint of the original cut. A starting point of this path has ambient distance at most $L$ from $T$, and each graph step changes ambient distance by at most one. That endpoint would be within $L+2r$ of $T$, contradicting <a href="#eq:amplification-cut-clearance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:amplification-cut-clearance">[eq:amplification-cut-clearance]</a> for large $n$. Thus the graph neighborhood lies in $A$, as claimed. ◻

</details>

The global gap enters through the marginal-tail estimate, the construction of positive constraints, and the excited-state decay. Its final entropy comparison is confined to the target dimension. The next section constructs tiles whose enlarged graph neighborhoods avoid all previously used tiles of the same family, so that Proposition <a href="#prop:amplification" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:amplification">32</a> can be applied repeatedly.

<a id="sec:geometry"></a>
### Two families of regions and the area bound

The amplified collar estimate controls the mutual information between one region and any collection of sites outside its collar. To use it in an entropy chain, we need to divide $A$ into two families: within each family, the collar of a region must avoid all regions that precede it. We group cells in distance layers into primary tiles separated by sparse strips. Filling the strips with suitable labels leaves only point contacts between regions of the same family. We separate those contacts by recursively replacing small squares around them. The sites left at the end of this construction, and all the mutual-information errors, will be bounded by the number of cut edges.

The construction takes place in the ambient plane. Its use of ambient distance only supplies sufficient conditions for separation in the induced graph: every graph path of length $r$ has ambient displacement at most $r$. We never require an ambiently short path to exist in the domain.

<a id="pm-h-60"></a>
#### The entropy cancellation

We first isolate the elementary reason that two families suffice. This also specifies precisely the separation property that the geometry must provide.

<a id="stmt-geometry-cancellation"></a>
<div id="geometry:cancellation" class="lemma">

**Lemma 33** (Two-family entropy cancellation). *Let $\psi$ be a pure state on a finite tensor product with site set $\Lambda$. Suppose that $$A=D\mathbin{\dot\cup}\bigcup_{i\in\mathcal I_0}X_i
       \mathbin{\dot\cup}\bigcup_{i\in\mathcal I_1}X_i
 \subseteq\Lambda$$ is a partition into disjoint sets, and fix an order on each finite index set $\mathcal I_f$, $f\in\{0,1\}$. Write $B=\Lambda\setminus A$. If $$I_\psi\left(X_i:B\cup
       \bigcup_{\substack{j\in\mathcal I_f\\j<i}}X_j\right)
 \le \varepsilon_i
 \qquad(i\in\mathcal I_f),$$ then $$S_\psi(A)\le S_\psi(D)+\frac12\sum_i\varepsilon_i.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-geometry-cancellation"><summary>Proof of stmt-geometry-cancellation</summary>

*Proof.* Write $A_f=\bigcup_{i\in\mathcal I_f}X_i$ and $E_f=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_f}\varepsilon_i$. The entropy chain rule and purity give $$S_\psi(BA_f)
 \ge S_\psi(B)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_f}S_\psi(X_i)-E_f
 =S_\psi(A)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_f}S_\psi(X_i)-E_f.$$ On the other hand, purity and subadditivity give $$S_\psi(BA_f)=S_\psi(DA_{1-f})
 \le S_\psi(D)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{1-f}}S_\psi(X_i).$$ Adding the inequalities for $f=0$ and $f=1$ cancels every individual tile entropy and proves the claim. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-61"></a>
#### The geometric statement

Keep the exponent $\beta=1-2\cdot10^{-6}$ from Proposition <a href="#prop:amplification" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:amplification">32</a>, and put <a id="geometry:exponents"></a>$$\label{geometry:exponents}
 \delta_0=2\cdot10^{-7},\qquad
 \zeta=1-\frac{\delta_0}{2},\qquad
 \rho_0=\frac{1+\beta}{2},\qquad
 \ell=10^{-5}.$$ The inequalities we shall use are <a id="geometry:exponent-gaps"></a>$$\label{geometry:exponent-gaps}
 (1+2\delta_0)\beta<\zeta<1,\qquad
 (1+2\delta_0)(1-\ell)<1,\qquad
 1-\ell<\beta<\rho_0<1.$$ All their gaps are fixed positive numbers. Thresholds depending on these gaps may therefore be chosen independently of $\Lambda$ and $A$.

A *birth region* below is the bounded closed planar region assigned to a tile when that tile is created. Later steps only delete points from that tile. Its *actual region* is the interior of its birth region remaining after all deletions. Different pieces with the same tile identifier are treated as one region; neither a birth region nor an actual region is required to be connected. Its ambient lattice template is the intersection of its birth region with $\mathbb Z^2$. We distinguish the two family labels $0,1$ from the two sides $A,\Lambda\setminus A$ of the physical cut.

<a id="stmt-prop-two-families"></a>
<div id="prop:two-families" class="proposition">

**Proposition 34** (Two families with separated birth templates). *Fix the constants $D_0$ and $C_{\mathrm{tpl}}$ in Definition <a href="#scanner:template" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:template">27</a>, and a lower scale threshold $n_*\ge1$. There is a constant $C$ with the following property. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite induced subgraph of the square lattice, let $A\subseteq\Lambda$, and suppose that $b=|\partial_\Lambda A|>0$. Let $Z$ be the set of endpoints of those cut edges.*

*There are a set $D\subseteq A$, a finite ordered collection of disjoint nonempty sets $X_i\subseteq A$, labels $f_i\in\{0,1\}$, ambient templates $T_i\subset\mathbb Z^2$, and integers $n_i\ge n_*$ such that:*

1.  *$A=D\mathbin{\dot\cup}\bigcup_iX_i$ and $|D|\le Cb$.*

2.  *$X_i\subseteq A\cap T_i$. Each $T_i$ is a template of Definition <a href="#scanner:template" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:template">27</a>: it is a union of $N_i$ lattice samples of closed convex rectangles or triangles with side slopes $0,\infty,1,-1$, each of sup-norm diameter at most $s_i$, where $$\mathop{\mathrm{diam}}_\infty T_i\le n_i,\qquad
     n_i\ge C_{\mathrm{tpl}}N_i(s_i+1),\qquad
     \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(T_i,Z)>4D_0s_i.$$ Moreover $L_i=\lfloor n_i^{1-\ell}\rfloor\le s_i$.*

<a id="geometry:cut-clearance"></a>
<a id="geometry:ordered-clearance"></a>
3.  *The templates satisfy $$\begin{aligned}
     \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(T_i,Z)&>2n_i^\beta,\label{geometry:cut-clearance}\\
     \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty\left(T_i,
           \bigcup_{\substack{j<i\\f_j=f_i}}X_j\right)
           &>2n_i^\beta.\label{geometry:ordered-clearance}
    \end{aligned}$$ As usual, the distance to the empty set is infinite.*

4.  *The scale losses are summable: $$\sum_i n_i^{-100}\le Cb.$$*

*The constant $C$ may depend on the fixed template constants and on $n_*$, but not on the domain or cut.*

</div>

We prove the proposition in stages. First we construct layers with sparse connecting strips. Next we remove their same-family vertex contacts. Finally we verify separation for the entire birth templates, not merely for the smaller actual regions.

<a id="pm-h-62"></a>
#### Layers and sparse strips

Fix a translated origin $$o=(\sqrt2,\sqrt3).$$ Each of $o_1,o_2,o_1+o_2,o_1-o_2$ is nonintegral. On every dyadic scale $r=2^k$, use the half-open cells $$C_{k,z}=o+r\bigl(z+[0,1)^2\bigr),\qquad z\in\mathbb Z^2.$$ These grids are nested. Half-open cells determine indices; their closures will determine birth regions. Choose an integer $C_0$ sufficiently large compared with $D_0$, for example $C_0>100(D_0+1)$, and define $$\mathcal Z_k=\{z:C_{k,z}\cap Z\ne\varnothing\},\qquad
 N_k=\bigcup_{\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(z,\mathcal Z_k)\le C_0}C_{k,z}.$$ Here the distance in the subscript is the sup distance between integer cell indices. Passing to parents shows that $N_k\subseteq N_{k+1}$: if two child indices differ by at most $C_0$ in each coordinate, their parent indices also differ by at most $C_0$. The sets $N_k$ exhaust the plane, since $Z\ne\varnothing$ and $C_0\ge2$.

<a id="geometry:layer-distance"></a>
For a lower index $k_0$ to be fixed later, regard $N_{k_0}$ as one *dummy tile*, labeled by the parity of $k_0-1$. Its points will initially be exceptional. For $k\ge k_0$, the layer $$D_k=N_{k+1}\setminus N_k$$ is a union of cells of side $r=2^k$. There are at most $C|Z|\le Cb$ of these cells: $N_{k+1}$ has at most $(2C_0+1)^2|Z|$ cells of side $2r$, each of which has four children. The cell-index definition also gives $$\label{geometry:layer-distance}
 C_0r\le\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(x,Z)\le2(C_0+1)r
 \qquad(x\in\overline{D_k}).$$ For the lower bound, a cell outside $N_k$ differs from every endpoint-occupied cell by at least $C_0+1$ in one coordinate. For the upper bound use its parent in $N_{k+1}$.

<a id="geometry:nonadjacent"></a>
The function $x\mapsto\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(x,Z)$ is 1-Lipschitz. Consequently, if $h\ge k+2$, then $$\label{geometry:nonadjacent}
 \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\infty(\overline{D_k},\overline{D_h})
 \ge C_0 2^h-2(C_0+1)2^k
 \ge \frac{C_0-1}{2}\,2^h.$$ Thus only the same layer or a neighboring layer can occur near a region whose size is much smaller than its layer scale.

In $D_k$ put $$s_k=2^{\lfloor(1+\delta_0)k\rfloor},\qquad
 t_k=2^{\lfloor\zeta k\rfloor}.$$ For sufficiently large $k_0$, we have $t_k\mid r\mid s_k$ and $t_k\ll r\ll s_k$, uniformly as $k\to\infty$. Here $r$ is the layer-cell scale, $s_k$ is the pitch used to group fragments into primary tiles, and $t_k$ will be the width of the strips separating those tiles. The larger pitch makes the strips sparse within a layer; the $r$-cells will later supply the small pieces in each primary’s template. The fine cells of side $t_k$ have origin $o$. Choose two residue classes modulo $s_k/t_k$, one for each coordinate. A fine cell is called a *belt cell* if either of its two indices lies in the corresponding selected residue class. The remaining fine cells lie in open pitch interiors, each a square between successive belt strips. For each such pitch interior, give all its fragments in $D_k$ one primary-tile identifier and the label $k\bmod2$.

<a id="geometry:belt-count"></a>
The shifts can be chosen so that few belt cells meet the layer. Indeed, the layer contains at most $Cb(r/t_k)^2$ fine cells before any shift is chosen. Under a uniform choice of the two residue classes, each is a belt cell with probability at most $2t_k/s_k$. Hence some shift satisfies $$\label{geometry:belt-count}
 \#\{\text{belt cells in }D_k\}
 \le Cb\frac{r^2}{s_kt_k}
 \le Cb\,2^{-k\delta_0/2}.$$ We fix such a shift in each layer. This is an averaging argument on a predetermined collection of cells; no property of the state enters it. The geometric decay in $k$ absorbs any fixed power of $k$. Below, <a href="#geometry:descendant-count" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:descendant-count">[geometry:descendant-count]</a> will bound the number of repairs descended from one contact by just such a power, so sparse strips also control the total number of tiles created by the repairs.

<a id="geometry:primary-pieces"></a>
Each $r$-cell meets only a bounded number of pitch interiors, so there are at most $Cb$ primary tiles in a layer. The birth region of one primary is a union of at most $$\label{geometry:primary-pieces}
 C(s_k/r+2)^2$$ closed rectangles of sup-norm diameter at most $r$, obtained as closures of the intersections of that pitch interior with the $r$-cells of the layer. Its whole sup-norm diameter is at most $s_k$. Distinct primaries in the same layer are separated by a belt strip of width at least $t_k$. Primaries in adjacent layers have opposite labels; primaries of the same label in different layers satisfy <a href="#geometry:nonadjacent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:nonadjacent">[geometry:nonadjacent]</a>. Figure <a href="#geometry:layer-picture" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="geometry:layer-picture">3</a> shows why a primary can have several components even though it occupies a single pitch interior.

<figure id="geometry:layer-picture">

<figcaption>A schematic portion of one ambient layer, not to scale. Dashed lines mark the $r$-cells. The thick square is one pitch cell; its interior after removing the belt strips has side $s_{k} − t_{k}$. All blue fragments in that interior share the primary identifier $P$, even when disconnected. The neighboring fragment has identifier $Q$. Both primaries have family label $k mod  2$; the orange belt cells are filled and labeled in the next step. The drawing concerns the ambient layer $D_{k}$, before intersection with the physical set $A$.</figcaption>
</figure>

```text
A 2D diagram of a square pitch cell of total side length $s_k$, marked at the bottom by a double-headed arrow labeled "pitch $s_k$". The area is overlaid with a regular square grid of $r$-cells indicated by dashed lines, with cell width marked at the top by a double-headed arrow labeled "$r$". Orange-shaded rectangular strips of width $t_k$ (indicated by a double-headed arrow labeled "$t_k$" near the bottom right) run along the perimeter, representing belt cells. In the pitch interior, several disconnected shaded blue regions are labeled "$P$", representing fragments of a single primary tile, while an adjacent blue region is labeled "$Q$". A legend to the right displays: a gray square labeled "$D_k$: shaded $r$-cells", a blue square labeled "primary fragments", and an orange square labeled "belt cells".
```


<a id="pm-h-63"></a>
#### Filling the belts

The remaining construction colors the belt cells while making every positive-length interface between different tile identifiers join opposite labels. Point contacts will be dealt with separately.

Adjacent layer fine meshes have side ratio either 1 or 2. They have a common translated dyadic origin, including after the pitch shifts, which were by multiples of their fine-cell sides. Divide a side of a belt cell at any corner of an opposing cell. A larger side can be divided only at its midpoint. Along each resulting elementary segment, the opposing region is either one primary or dummy tile, or one elementary segment of another belt cell. A layer boundary cannot change in the interior of such a segment: layer edges lie on the coarser dyadic grids.

Join the center of each belt cell to the endpoints of its elementary segments. This makes a fan of at most eight triangles, with edges of slopes $0,\infty,1,-1$. A triangle facing a primary or dummy tile receives the opposite label. On a segment shared by two belt cells, assign any opposite pair of labels to its two incident triangles, consistently on both sides. Within each belt cell merge each cyclic run of consecutive triangles with the same label into one tile identifier. Distinct runs remain distinct identifiers; if all labels agree, the whole cell is one tile.

Every positive-length interface between distinct identifiers now joins opposite labels. Across a cell side this follows from the assignment; inside a fan it follows from merging equal-label neighbors. Primaries were already separated in the same layer, and adjacent-layer primaries have opposite labels. Thus a same-label contact between distinct tiles can only be a point, and every such contact involves a belt cell.

Mark the center, the four corners, and the four side midpoints of every belt cell. Some midpoint marks are unnecessary for its fan, but adding them simplifies the recursion. Deduplicate coincident marks, assigning a mark $v$ the scale $S_v$ equal to the smallest side length of a belt cell that marked it. There are at most nine times as many initial marks as belt cells.

<a id="stmt-geometry-initial-stars"></a>
<div id="geometry:initial-stars" class="lemma">

**Lemma 35** (Isolated stars of the initial mesh). *There is an absolute constant $a_0>0$, independent of the layer and the chosen shifts, such that, on taking $k_0$ sufficiently large:*

1.  *Distinct marks $v,w$ satisfy $\lVert v-w\rVert_\infty\ge a_0\max(S_v,S_w)$.*

2.  *In the square $v+[-a_0S_v,a_0S_v]^2$, all active boundaries are straight rays from $v$ in the eight axis and diagonal directions. Each sector between consecutive active rays has one tile identifier, and consecutive sectors have opposite labels. If there is no active ray, the square is in one tile.*

*An active boundary here means an interface of distinct identifiers; seams removed by a merge are not boundaries.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-geometry-initial-stars"><summary>Proof of stmt-geometry-initial-stars</summary>

*Proof.* Consider a belt cell of side $t=t_k$. In its $10t$-neighborhood only its own and adjacent layers can occur, by <a href="#geometry:nonadjacent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:nonadjacent">[geometry:nonadjacent]</a> and $t_k/2^k\to0$. All fine-cell sides there are $t/2,t$, or $2t$. Cell corners, fan centers, and side midpoints therefore lie on the affine mesh $o+(t/4)\mathbb Z^2$. All active lines have one of the four allowed slopes and intercepts on this mesh. Marks have local scales comparable to $t$. Distinct marks have distance at least $t/4$, and a supporting line that does not contain a given mark is at sup distance at least $t/8$ from it. The same bounds apply to the nearest other endpoint of an incident segment. Choosing $a_0$ small gives both assertions locally. Apply this argument at the larger scale for a pair of nearby marks; pairs outside the local neighborhood already satisfy the asserted separation.

The preceding coloring shows that two sectors separated by an active ray have opposite labels. Coincident boundary segments or inactive seams are counted only once, so this describes the actual tile regions near the mark. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-64"></a>
#### Removing point contacts at successively smaller scales

The purpose of the next construction is to make the birth template of each newly created tile avoid the final actual sets of earlier tiles of the same label. Removing points only from the new tile would not provide that property. We remove a square from every old identifier incident with the mark before creating its replacement.

<a id="geometry:trim-radius"></a>
<a id="geometry:trim-margins"></a>
Choose a fixed stopping scale $S_*$ sufficiently large that, for every $S\ge S_*$, the dyadic halfside $$\label{geometry:trim-radius}
 d(S)=2^{\lfloor\rho_0\log_2 S\rfloor}$$ satisfies $$\label{geometry:trim-margins}
 \tfrac12S^{\rho_0}\le d(S)\le S^{\rho_0},\qquad
 d(S)\le\frac{a_0}{1000}S.$$ We will increase $S_*$ later to accommodate the collar estimate. Choose $k_0$ so that all initial mark scales are at least $S_*$. At each generation perform the following operations simultaneously at every active mark $(v,S)$:

1.  Remove the closed square $Q_v=v+[-d(S),d(S)]^2$ from every old tile identifier.

2.  If $d(S)<S_*$, leave its interior unassigned and declare it a terminal exceptional square.

3.  Otherwise, continue the incident active rays through the square to its center. In each resulting sector give the new region the label opposite to that of the corresponding exterior sector, with a new identifier for each sector. If there are no rays, use one opposite-label square. Mark the center, corners, and side midpoints of $Q_v$, all at scale $d(S)$, for the next generation.

A sector with angle exceeding $\pi$ need not be convex; it is a union of at most eight of the triangles from the center to side corners and midpoints. Thus all replacement birth regions retain the required finite description. Every old ray meets the square perimeter at a corner or side midpoint. Figure <a href="#geometry:repair-picture" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="geometry:repair-picture">4</a> illustrates the label reversal and the marks used at the next generation.

<figure id="geometry:repair-picture">

<figcaption>A four-sector example of the repair. The square around the contact is removed from every old tile, and its new sectors receive the opposite labels. Positive-length interfaces still join opposite labels. Any same-label contacts involving the new tiles occur among the nine marked points; the next, smaller removal separates them. The proof also allows any configuration of the eight permitted ray directions with opposite labels in consecutive sectors.</figcaption>
</figure>
