We now verify that this procedure continues with uniform geometric constants. In particular, neither the separation constant nor the isolation radius is allowed to deteriorate with the number of generations.

<a id="stmt-geometry-repair-induction"></a>
<div id="geometry:repair-induction" class="lemma">

**Lemma 36** (Uniform repair induction). *For a sufficiently small fixed choice of $a_0$ and the corresponding threshold $S_*$, every active mark $(v,S)$ at every generation has a terminal-square-free isolated star $v+[-a_0S,a_0S]^2$ with the properties of Lemma <a href="#geometry:initial-stars" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="geometry:initial-stars">35</a>. Distinct active marks satisfy the same separation inequality. The simultaneous removal squares are disjoint. Each replacement has opposite labels across every positive-length interface of distinct identifiers, and its same-label contacts with old remnants or peer replacements occur only at marks of the next generation. Every descendant mark and every descendant birth region of a mark $(v,S)$ lies within sup distance $2d(S)$ of $v$. Each branch terminates after finitely many generations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-geometry-repair-induction"><summary>Proof of stmt-geometry-repair-induction</summary>

*Proof.* Suppose the assertions hold at one generation. By <a href="#geometry:trim-margins" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:trim-margins">[geometry:trim-margins]</a>, the squares of radius $6d(S)$ are contained in their parent stars. They are also disjoint from all other current removal squares. Indeed for parent marks $(v,S),(w,T)$, $$\lVert v-w\rVert_\infty\ge a_0\max(S,T),\qquad
 6d(S)+d(T)\le \frac{7a_0}{1000}\max(S,T).$$ Thus each modification sees only its parent’s radial boundaries.

Across a new perimeter segment away from ray hits, the new interior label was chosen opposite to the exterior label. Across an interior ray, the two labels remain opposite because the two exterior labels were opposite. All other positive-length interfaces are unchanged. Contacts not lying in the relative interior of one of these segments are among the center, corners, or side midpoints of the new square. This proves the coloring and contact assertions.

Normalize one removal square to $[-1,1]^2$. Its post-replacement boundaries are subsets of the original eight radial rays together with the four lines supporting this square. The possible new marks are the nine points of $\{-1,0,1\}^2$. Every nonincident supporting line stays at a fixed positive distance from a mark, and every other endpoint stays at distance at least one. Thus a fixed sufficiently small $a_0$ gives an isolated radial star at each child, on the child’s scale $d(S)$. This is the same finite line configuration at every generation, so no iteration of a shrinking constant is involved.

Two children of the same parent are at least $d(S)$ apart. For children of different parents their separation is at least $$a_0\max(S,T)-d(S)-d(T)
 \ge \frac{a_0}{2}\max(S,T),$$ which is larger than $a_0\max(d(S),d(T))$ by <a href="#geometry:trim-margins" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:trim-margins">[geometry:trim-margins]</a>. Their isolated-star squares therefore satisfy the original separation invariant as well.

The child stars lie inside the parent star. Consequently they avoid all terminal squares from earlier generations. A terminal square created at another parent in the current generation is excluded by the same cross-parent distance estimate. For a direct statement covering all later generations, each successive child displacement is at most the preceding removal radius, and subsequent radii shrink by the fixed factor at most $a_0/1000$. Their sum, including the radius of the final descendant birth square, is less than $2d(S)$. Subtrees of distinct parents are therefore separated by the preceding inequalities, even if one subtree has already terminated. This proves the asserted terminal-square avoidance and descendant bound.

Finally, as long as a branch continues, its successive scales satisfy $S_{j+1}=d(S_j)\le S_j^{\rho_0}$ with $\rho_0<1$. After finitely many steps the computed next halfside is below $S_*$, and that removal is terminal. This completes the induction. ◻

</details>

All geometric edges avoid lattice sites. Initially their vertices are in $o+\mathbb Z^2$ because $r,s_k,t_k$ are dyadic integers, and the halfsizes and midpoints used are integral. In the recursion each new center, corner, and midpoint is obtained by adding an integer vector to the preceding center; the halfside $d(S)$ is an integer. Enlarge $S_*$ once so that a terminal halfside produced from $S\ge S_*$ is still at least two. Every supporting line consequently has equation $$x_1=o_1+m,\quad x_2=o_2+m,\quad
 x_1+x_2=o_1+o_2+m,\quad\text{or}\quad
 x_1-x_2=o_1-o_2+m,\qquad m\in\mathbb Z.$$ None contains a point of $\mathbb Z^2$. We may therefore use open actual tile regions and closed birth regions without any convention for assigning a lattice site on an interface. The final open tile regions, the unaltered part of the dummy region, and terminal-square interiors partition all lattice sites.

<a id="pm-h-65"></a>
#### Separation from earlier actual regions

Order tile identifiers as follows: all primaries first, all initial belt tiles second, and then the replacement tiles by their generation of birth. Ties within each class can be broken arbitrarily. The dummy tile is excluded from this order. Primaries already have the required same-label separation from other primaries. The next lemma handles all remaining identifiers and explains why the order uses actual earlier regions.

<a id="stmt-geometry-birth-separation"></a>
<div id="geometry:birth-separation" class="lemma">

**Lemma 37** (Birth-template separation). *There is a fixed $c_1>0$ such that the following holds. Let $\mathcal B$ be the closed birth region of an initial belt tile of side scale $u=t_k$, or of a replacement tile whose removal square has halfside $u$. Then its distance from the final actual region of every earlier or peer identifier of the same label is at least $c_1u^{\rho_0}$. A peer means another initial belt tile, or another replacement born at the same generation, respectively.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-geometry-birth-separation"><summary>Proof of stmt-geometry-birth-separation</summary>

*Proof.* At the birth of an initial belt tile, compare its closure with the primary and belt closures at that time. At the birth of a replacement, compare it with the old remnants *after* that generation’s removal squares have been cut out, and with the peer replacements. Each final actual region is a subset of the corresponding compared region. In particular an ancestor is compared after its square has been removed; its original birth region need not be disjoint from the new one.

Restrict attention to a closed box obtained by enlarging the tile’s cell or removal square by $2u$ in each direction. Points outside this box are at distance at least $2u$ from the birth region. Translate by its cell corner, or by its removal center, and rescale lengths by $u$. Only finitely many local pairs of closed regions can arise:

- For belts, the nearby active lines and endpoints lie on the affine quarter mesh, with their four prescribed slopes. In a bounded box there are only finitely many such lines and endpoints. The local closures are unions of faces of their arrangement; allowing all possible identifier groupings still leaves only finitely many pairs of unions. We classify only the restrictions to this box: disconnected pieces of an identifier outside it do not change the local pattern.

- For a replacement, the enlarged box lies in the isolated star of its parent, by <a href="#geometry:trim-margins" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:trim-margins">[geometry:trim-margins]</a>. It sees only the old radial layout and the new square and sectors. These lie on a fixed finite arrangement in the rescaled coordinates. Other parents’ simultaneous modifications do not enter this box.

Thus there is a common positive scale for the isolation neighborhoods used in all these comparisons.

The two compared closures of the same label have no positive-length interface. Their intersections, if any, are contact marks by the belt construction or Lemma <a href="#geometry:repair-induction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="geometry:repair-induction">36</a>. At a belt contact the mark scale is comparable with $u$ (neighboring belt scales differ by at most two); at a replacement contact it is $u$. Choose disjoint open contact squares of radius $\lambda u$ inside the isolated stars, for a fixed sufficiently small $\lambda>0$.

First consider pairs of points $(x,y)$ in the two compared closures that do not both belong to the same open contact square. This condition specifies a closed subset of the compact product of the two local closures. On it the distance $\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty$ has a positive minimum: if the minimum were zero, $x=y$ would be a common contact, and both points would belong to its open contact square. Since the list of rescaled patterns is finite, the minimum is uniformly at least $c_2u$ whenever this subset is nonempty.

<a id="geometry:angular-gap"></a>
It remains to consider $x,y$ in one contact star centered at $v$. Inside that star each closure is a union of closed radial sectors. Their direction sets are disjoint. A shared direction would give a shared ray segment, contrary to the absence of positive-length same-label contacts. Their boundary directions are among the eight axis and diagonal directions, so the angle between their direction sets is at least $\pi/4$. Elementary Euclidean geometry, followed by comparison of Euclidean and sup norms, gives $$\label{geometry:angular-gap}
 \lVert x-y\rVert_\infty
 \ge c_3\max\{\lVert x-v\rVert_\infty,\lVert y-v\rVert_\infty\}.$$ For example, the squared Euclidean distance between radial vectors of lengths $a,b$ and angle $\theta\ge\pi/4$ is $(a-b)^2+2ab(1-\cos\theta)$, which bounds a fixed multiple of $\max(a,b)^2$.

At the immediately following trim, the compared old or peer identifier loses a square about $v$ of radius at least $c_4u^{\rho_0}$, by <a href="#geometry:trim-radius" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:trim-radius">[geometry:trim-radius]</a> and comparability of mark scales. This removal also occurs if the square is terminal. That identifier only shrinks afterward. Thus a point $y$ in its final actual region has $\lVert y-v\rVert_\infty\ge c_4u^{\rho_0}$, and <a href="#geometry:angular-gap" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:angular-gap">[geometry:angular-gap]</a> supplies the required lower bound for pairs inside the contact star. Together with the preceding compactness estimate and the exterior-of-box estimate this proves the lemma. ◻

</details>

The lemma compares the entire new birth region with an older actual region. Later deletions from the new tile are irrelevant to this estimate. This is the form needed for applying the collar estimate to its untrimmed template and then discarding part of that template.

<a id="pm-h-66"></a>
#### Counting exceptional sites and verifying the templates

<a id="geometry:descendant-count"></a>
<a id="geometry:total-repairs"></a>
Let an initial mark have scale $S$. Along a branch, $\log S_j\le\rho_0^j\log S$ until termination. Its depth is therefore at most $$C+C\log\log(e^e+S).$$ There are at most nine children per mark. Consequently the number of marks and replacements descended from this initial mark is at most $$\label{geometry:descendant-count}
 C\bigl(\log(S+2)\bigr)^{C}.$$ The constants are fixed; their magnitude is immaterial for a size-independent area bound. The scale of a mark initially belonging to layer $k$ is comparable with $t_k$, and hence its logarithm is at most $C(k+1)$. By <a href="#geometry:belt-count" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:belt-count">[geometry:belt-count]</a>, the total number of belt tiles, marks, and replacements is bounded by $$\label{geometry:total-repairs}
 Cb\sum_{k\ge k_0}2^{-k\delta_0/2}(k+1)^C\le C'b.$$ In particular this total is finite, even before restricting the construction to the finite domain.

Each terminal square has halfside below the fixed $S_*$ and therefore contains at most $C S_*^2$ lattice sites. The dummy region has at most $C|Z|$ cells of the fixed side $2^{k_0}$ and hence at most $Cb$ lattice sites. Let $D$ be the sites of $A$ that remain in the dummy identifier or lie in terminal squares. Sites overwritten by a replacement are no longer counted as dummy sites. Equations <a href="#geometry:descendant-count" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:descendant-count">[geometry:descendant-count]</a> and <a href="#geometry:total-repairs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:total-repairs">[geometry:total-repairs]</a> give <a id="geometry:bad-sites"></a>$$\label{geometry:bad-sites}
 |D|\le Cb.$$ This counts ambient sites and then intersects with $A$. Missing sites, holes, thin parts, and disconnected components of $\Lambda$ can only reduce the count.

<a id="geometry:primary-limits"></a>
We now assign scanner scales to the birth templates. Let $T=\mathcal B\cap\mathbb Z^2$ for a birth region $\mathcal B$. For a primary in layer $k$, take <a id="geometry:primary-scale"></a>$$\label{geometry:primary-scale}
 s_0=r=2^k,\qquad n=\left\lceil C_P r^{1+2\delta_0}\right\rceil.$$ By <a href="#geometry:primary-pieces" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:primary-pieces">[geometry:primary-pieces]</a>, it has at most $N_0\le C(s_k/r+2)^2\le C r^{2\delta_0}$ rectangular pieces, each of sup-norm diameter at most $s_0$. Choosing $C_P$ large ensures $$n\ge C_{\mathrm{tpl}}N_0(s_0+1),\qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{diam}}_\infty T\le s_k\le n.$$ The birth template has endpoint distance at least $C_0r$, so the safe clearance in Definition <a href="#scanner:template" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:template">27</a> follows from the choice of $C_0$. The exponent inequalities give, uniformly over primaries, $$\label{geometry:primary-limits}
 L=\lfloor n^{1-\ell}\rfloor=o(r),\qquad
 n^\beta=o(t_k),\qquad n^\beta=o(r).$$

For a belt tile take $u=t_k$, $s_0=u$, and $n=\lceil C_Bu\rceil$. It is a union of at most eight of the closed fan triangles. For a replacement whose removal halfside is $u$, take $s_0=2u$ and $n=\lceil C_Bu\rceil$. Subdivision into the triangles from the center to corners and midpoints again uses at most eight pieces, including for a wide sector or a homogeneous square. Choose $C_B$ large enough for all of these templates to satisfy $n\ge C_{\mathrm{tpl}}N_0(s_0+1)$ and $\mathop{\mathrm{diam}}_\infty T\le n$. In both cases $L=o(u)$.

Their cut clearance remains much larger than their size. An initial belt cell in $D_k$ has endpoint distance at least $C_0r$. A mark on its closure has the same lower bound. By Lemma <a href="#geometry:repair-induction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="geometry:repair-induction">36</a>, every descendant lies within $2d(S)\le2t_k^{\rho_0}=o(t_k)$ of that mark. After increasing $k_0$, all its descendant birth templates therefore have endpoint distance at least $(C_0-1)r$. This also covers replacements extending into the dummy region. Since their side scales are at most $2t_k=o(r)$, their endpoint distance exceeds both $4D_0s_0$ and $2n^\beta$.

These checks establish the exact geometric hypotheses of Lemma <a href="#scanner:templates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="scanner:templates">28</a>. In particular, for every birth template, its dilated layers up to $L$ have the stipulated row and perimeter bounds, and the safe-box estimate yields the core and shell entropy bounds needed by Proposition <a href="#prop:collar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:collar">30</a>. The verification uses the finite union of convex pieces; no assertion that a primary, a sector run, or its intersection with $A$ is a rectangle is needed.

<a id="geometry:fine-clearance"></a>
For clarity, the relevant thresholds can be fixed in the following order. First fix $C_0,C_P,C_B$ and the absolute isolation constant. Next increase $S_*$ until <a href="#geometry:trim-margins" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:trim-margins">[geometry:trim-margins]</a> holds, all belt and replacement scanner scales are at least $n_*$, and $$\label{geometry:fine-clearance}
 c_1u^{\rho_0}>2\lceil C_Bu\rceil^\beta
 \qquad(u\ge S_*).$$ This is possible because $\rho_0>\beta$. Finally increase $k_0$ to ensure that initial belt scales exceed $S_*$, that all primary scales exceed $n_*$, and that all the uniform large-scale inequalities just used hold. For primaries this includes their same-layer gap $t_k>2n^\beta$, their nonadjacent-layer gaps, and <a href="#geometry:primary-limits" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:primary-limits">[geometry:primary-limits]</a>. Floors and ceilings only change fixed multiplicative constants.

We can now finish the geometric proposition. Retain just identifiers whose final actual regions meet $A$, and let $X_i$ be those intersections, ordered as above. There are finitely many, since these nonempty sets are pairwise disjoint subsets of a finite set. They partition $A\setminus
D$, and each lies in its birth template. Equations <a href="#geometry:layer-distance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:layer-distance">[geometry:layer-distance]</a>, <a href="#geometry:primary-limits" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:primary-limits">[geometry:primary-limits]</a>, and the descendant clearance prove <a href="#geometry:cut-clearance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:cut-clearance">[geometry:cut-clearance]</a>. For primaries, earlier same-label primaries are separated by $t_k$ in the same layer or by <a href="#geometry:nonadjacent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:nonadjacent">[geometry:nonadjacent]</a> in other layers. For belts and replacements, Lemma <a href="#geometry:birth-separation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="geometry:birth-separation">37</a> and <a href="#geometry:fine-clearance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:fine-clearance">[geometry:fine-clearance]</a> prove <a href="#geometry:ordered-clearance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:ordered-clearance">[geometry:ordered-clearance]</a>. Restricting an older actual region to $A$ preserves these lower bounds.

There are at most $Cb$ primaries per layer, and their scales satisfy $n\ge c2^{(1+2\delta_0)k}$. Their error sum is therefore bounded by $$Cb\sum_{k\ge k_0}2^{-100(1+2\delta_0)k}\le C'b.$$ The total number of other tiles is $O(b)$ by <a href="#geometry:total-repairs" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:total-repairs">[geometry:total-repairs]</a>, and each has $n\ge1$. Their error sum is also $O(b)$. This proves every assertion of Proposition <a href="#prop:two-families" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:two-families">34</a>.

<a id="pm-h-67"></a>
#### Proof of the area law

<details id="proof-stmt-geometry-birth-separation-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-geometry-birth-separation</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:area" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:area">1</a>.* The empty domain and the empty or full region have zero entropy. Put $b=|\partial_\Lambda A|$. If $b=0$, Lemma <a href="#lem:zero-boundary" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:zero-boundary">4</a> gives $S_\Omega(A)=0$.

Assume $b>0$. Choose $n_*$ large enough for Proposition <a href="#prop:collar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:collar">30</a> and Proposition <a href="#prop:amplification" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:amplification">32</a> with $M=100$ to apply to the templates of Proposition <a href="#prop:two-families" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:two-families">34</a>, uniformly with the stated template bounds. Increase it so that every radius $r$ supplied by amplification at scale $n\ge n_*$ satisfies $L+2r<n^\beta$. Let $D,X_i,T_i,n_i,f_i$ be the resulting geometric decomposition, and put $$S_i=A\cap\bigl(T_i+[-L_i,L_i]^2_{\mathbb Z}\bigr),\qquad
 J_i=(\Lambda\setminus A)\cup
       \bigcup_{\substack{j<i\\f_j=f_i}}X_j.$$ Here $[-L_i,L_i]^2_{\mathbb Z}$ denotes the integer square. For each $i$, let $r_i$ be the radius supplied by amplification, using the size, boundary, and information bounds from Proposition <a href="#prop:collar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:collar">30</a>. The resulting mutual-information estimate applies to $A\cap T_i$ against any sites outside the graph neighborhood $N_{2r_i}^{\Lambda}(S_i)$.

We verify this condition for the whole set $J_i$, rather than for its individual pieces. A graph path of length at most $2r_i$ from $S_i$ stays within ambient distance $L_i+2r_i<n_i^\beta$ of $T_i$. Equation <a href="#geometry:ordered-clearance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:ordered-clearance">[geometry:ordered-clearance]</a> excludes every earlier same-family $X_j$ jointly. Such a path also cannot reach $\Lambda\setminus A$: its first crossing of the cut would put an endpoint of a cut edge within that ambient distance of $T_i$, contradicting <a href="#geometry:cut-clearance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="geometry:cut-clearance">[geometry:cut-clearance]</a>. Thus $$J_i\subseteq\Lambda\setminus N_{2r_i}^{\Lambda}(S_i).$$ Proposition <a href="#prop:amplification" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:amplification">32</a> and monotonicity under discarding part of its first system yield $$I_\Omega(X_i:J_i)
 \le I_\Omega(A\cap T_i:J_i)\le C n_i^{-100}.$$ These estimates all concern the same original state $\Omega$, although the auxiliary construction used to prove each estimate may differ.

Apply Lemma <a href="#geometry:cancellation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="geometry:cancellation">33</a> to the two labels. Since each site has dimension $q$, $$S_\Omega(A)
 \le |D|\log q+\frac C2\sum_i n_i^{-100}
 \le C' b.$$ Every choice of threshold and every constant in this proof depends only on the fixed local dimension, interaction range and norm bound, and spectral gap. None depends on the size, shape, connectedness, or holes of $\Lambda$, or on the choice of $A$. This proves the theorem. ◻

</details>

    {
      "caption": "One history and one conditional choice in a round. Arrows point toward the root and show metric evaluation; every internal vertex uses its specified geometric mean. Dotted arrows abbreviate whole paths, not single edges. The same interpolation parameter $p$ is used at every history. Trace adjoints of normalized derivatives carry states in the reverse direction.",
      "figure_id": "transport:tree-figure",
      "pdf_page": 46,
      "source_evidence": [
        {
          "anchor": "transport:tree-figure",
          "exact_quote": "One history and one conditional choice in a round.  Arrows\npoint toward the root and show metric evaluation; every internal\nvertex uses its specified geometric mean.  Dotted arrows abbreviate\nwhole paths, not single edges.  The same interpo",
          "source_object": "fig:0001"
        }
      ],
      "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1cm,y=1cm,font=\\small,>=Stealth]\n \\node (root) at (0,0) {$\\mathcal M(p)$};\n \\node[align=center] (node) at (4,0) {$A_h\\#_p B_h$};\n \\node (old) at (7,1.2) {$A_h$};\n \\node (choice) at (7,-1.2) {$B_h$};\n \\node (new) at (11,-1.2) {$A_{h,c}$};\n \\draw[->,densely dotted] (node)--node[above,align=center]\n   {history path\\\\product $w_h$}(root);\n \\draw[->] (old)--node[above left] {$1-p$}(node);\n \\draw[->] (choice)--node[below left] {$p$}(node);\n \\draw[->,densely dotted] (new)--node[above,align=center]\n   {choice path\\\\product $q_{c\\mid h}$}(choice);\n \\node[above=3pt of old] {$\\pi_{(h,\\mathrm{old})}=(1-p)w_h$};\n \\node[below=3pt of new] {$\\pi_{(h,c,\\mathrm{new})}=pw_hq_{c\\mid h}$};\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "A tree diagram oriented horizontally with arrows directed leftward toward the root $\\mathcal{M}(p)$. An intermediate vertex is labeled $A_h \\#_p B_h$, connected to $\\mathcal{M}(p)$ on the left by a horizontal dotted arrow labeled above with \"history path / product $w_h$\". From $A_h \\#_p B_h$, two solid edges diverge to the right with arrows pointing toward $A_h \\#_p B_h$: an upper edge labeled $1 - p$ incoming from node $A_h$, which is labeled above by $\\pi_{(h,\\text{old})} = (1 - p)w_h$; and a lower edge labeled $p$ incoming from node $B_h$. Node $B_h$ is connected via a horizontal dotted arrow pointing left from node $A_{h,c}$, labeled above with \"choice path / product $q_{c|h}$\" and below with $\\pi_{(h,c,\\text{new})} = pw_h q_{c|h}$."
    },
    {
      "caption": "Schematic nominal depth partitions in two bands, not to scale. The horizontal coordinate records distance from the target, not a physical lattice direction. Dashed lines are the nominal fronts, and arrows show the fill directions. Charges may have assigned individual sites in the hatched intervals, so the actual sets $U, Y, V$ need not be depth intervals. The separated windows ensure that one support cannot split two bands.       "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[x=.83cm,y=1cm,font=\\small,>=Stealth]\n \\foreach \\y/\\leftfront/\\rightfront/\\band in\n   {1.25/3.2/6.2/{g},0/8.1/11.1/{g+1}}{\n  \\fill[blue!15] (0,\\y) rectangle (.9,{\\y+.65});\n  \\fill[green!12] (.9,\\y) rectangle (\\leftfront,{\\y+.65});\n  \\fill[yellow!22] (\\leftfront,\\y) rectangle (\\rightfront,{\\y+.65});\n  \\fill[gray!15] (\\rightfront,\\y) rectangle (13,{\\y+.65});\n  \\draw (0,\\y) rectangle (13,{\\y+.65});\n  \\draw (.9,\\y)--(.9,{\\y+.65});\n  \\draw[densely dashed] (\\leftfront,{\\y-.08})--(\\leftfront,{\\y+.83});\n  \\draw[densely dashed] (\\rightfront,{\\y-.08})--(\\rightfront,{\\y+.83});\n  \\fill[pattern=north east lines,pattern color=gray!65]\n       (\\leftfront,\\y) rectangle ({\\leftfront+.55},{\\y+.65});\n  \\fill[pattern=north east lines,pattern color=gray!65]\n       ({\\rightfront-.55},\\y) rectangle (\\rightfront,{\\y+.65});\n  \\node at (.45,{\\y+.325}) {$X$};\n  \\node at ({(.9+\\leftfront)/2},{\\y+.325}) {$U$};\n  \\node at ({(\\leftfront+\\rightfront)/2},{\\y+.325}) {$Y$};\n  \\node at ({(\\rightfront+13)/2},{\\y+.325}) {$V$};\n  \\node[anchor=east] at (-.15,{\\y+.325}) {band $\\band$};\n  \\draw[->] (\\leftfront,{\\y+.8})--({\\leftfront+.9},{\\y+.8});\n  \\draw[->] (\\rightfront,{\\y+.8})--({\\rightfront-.9},{\\y+.8});\n }\n \\draw[<->] (3.2,2.35)--node[above] {$D+O(r_0)$}(3.75,2.35);\n \\draw[->] (0,-.5)--(13,-.5) node[right] {depth};\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "Two horizontal strip diagrams representing \"band $g$\" (top) and \"band $g + 1$\" (bottom) aligned above a horizontal axis labeled \"depth\" with an arrow pointing right. Each strip is partitioned from left to right into four consecutive regions labeled $X$, $U$, $Y$, and $V$. Region $X$ is tinted light purple. Vertical dashed lines mark nominal fronts between $U$ and $Y$, and between $Y$ and $V$, each surrounded by a diagonally hatched rectangular interval. Horizontal arrows show fill directions: pointing rightward at the $U/Y$ front and leftward at the $Y/V$ front. Above band $g$, a double-headed horizontal arrow labeled $D + O(r_0)$ indicates the width of the nominal $Y$ window. In band $g + 1$, region $U$ is longer, shifting the $Y$ window to the right relative to band $g$."

      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.05, line width=.45pt]\n \\foreach \\x/\\y in {0/1,1/1,1/2,3/0,3/1,3/2,3/3,4/1,4/2}\n   {\\fill[blue!16] (\\x,\\y) rectangle +(1,1);}\n \\fill[orange!35] (0,1) rectangle (.25,2);\n \\fill[orange!35] (3,0) rectangle (4,.25);\n \\fill[orange!35] (4,1) rectangle (4.25,3);\n \\draw[step=1,gray!65,densely dashed] (0,0) grid (5,4);\n \\draw[thick] (0,0) rectangle (4,4);\n \\draw[orange!70!black] (.25,0)--(.25,4)\n                          (4.25,0)--(4.25,4)\n                          (0,.25)--(5,.25);\n \\node at (1.45,1.5) {$P$};\n \\node at (3.5,2.45) {$P$};\n \\node at (4.65,1.5) {$Q$};\n \\node[anchor=west] at (5.35,3.35) {$D_k$: shaded $r$-cells};\n \\fill[blue!16] (5.4,2.65) rectangle (5.7,2.95);\n \\node[anchor=west] at (5.85,2.8) {primary fragments};\n \\fill[orange!35] (5.4,2.05) rectangle (5.7,2.35);\n \\node[anchor=west] at (5.85,2.2) {belt cells};\n \\draw[<->] (0,-.4)--(4,-.4);\n \\node[below] at (2,-.4) {pitch $s_k$};\n \\draw[<->] (1,4.35)--(2,4.35);\n \\node[above] at (1.5,4.35) {$r$};\n \\draw[<->] (4,.65)--(4.25,.65);\n \\draw (4,.5)--(4,.85) (4.25,.5)--(4.25,.85);\n \\node[anchor=west] at (4.4,.65) {$t_k$};\n\\end{tikzpicture}",

      "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.45, line width=.45pt]\n \\begin{scope}[xshift=-1.7cm]\n  \\fill[blue!14] (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);\n  \\fill[orange!22] (0,0) rectangle (1,1);\n  \\fill[blue!14] (0,-1) rectangle (1,0);\n  \\fill[orange!22] (-1,-1) rectangle (0,0);\n  \\draw (-1,-1) rectangle (1,1);\n  \\draw (-1,0)--(1,0) (0,-1)--(0,1);\n  \\draw[dashed] (-.42,-.42) rectangle (.42,.42);\n  \\node at (-.68,.68) {$0$}; \\node at (.68,.68) {$1$};\n  \\node at (.68,-.68) {$0$}; \\node at (-.68,-.68) {$1$};\n  \\fill (0,0) circle (1.1pt);\n  \\node[below] at (0,-1.08) {An isolated contact};\n \\end{scope}\n \\begin{scope}[xshift=1.7cm]\n  \\fill[blue!14] (-1,0) rectangle (0,1);\n  \\fill[orange!22] (0,0) rectangle (1,1);\n  \\fill[blue!14] (0,-1) rectangle (1,0);\n  \\fill[orange!22] (-1,-1) rectangle (0,0);\n  \\fill[orange!22] (-.42,0) rectangle (0,.42);\n  \\fill[blue!14] (0,0) rectangle (.42,.42);\n  \\fill[orange!22] (0,-.42) rectangle (.42,0);\n  \\fill[blue!14] (-.42,-.42) rectangle (0,0);\n  \\draw (-1,-1) rectangle (1,1);\n  \\draw (-1,0)--(1,0) (0,-1)--(0,1);\n  \\draw (-.42,-.42) rectangle (.42,.42);\n  \\node at (-.68,.68) {$0$}; \\node at (.68,.68) {$1$};\n  \\node at (.68,-.68) {$0$}; \\node at (-.68,-.68) {$1$};\n  \\node at (-.22,.22) {$1$}; \\node at (.22,.22) {$0$};\n  \\node at (.22,-.22) {$1$}; \\node at (-.22,-.22) {$0$};\n  \\foreach \\x in {-.42,0,.42}\n   \\foreach \\y in {-.42,0,.42}\n    {\\fill (\\x,\\y) circle (.85pt);}\n  \\node[below] at (0,-1.08) {Replacement and next marks};\n \\end{scope}\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "Two side-by-side square diagrams showing contact repair:\nLeft diagram, subtitled \"An isolated contact\": A square partitioned into four quadrants meeting at a central point. The top-left and bottom-right quadrants are shaded light blue and labeled \"0\". The top-right and bottom-left quadrants are shaded light orange and labeled \"1\". A central dashed square with dashed ray extensions indicates the neighborhood around the contact point to be excised.\nRight diagram, subtitled \"Replacement and next marks\": The exterior four quadrants retain their original shading and labels (0, 1, 1, 0). The central excised square is replaced by four quadrants with reversed labels and colors: top-left is orange labeled \"1\", top-right is blue labeled \"0\", bottom-left is blue labeled \"0\", and bottom-right is orange labeled \"1\". Nine solid black circular dots mark the next generation scale points: one at the center of the square, four at the corners of the square, and four at the midpoints of the square's four edges."
